original: Looking through the comment section here, I agree to a large degree with the author's standpoint on many issues discussed. Points (1) through (4) in the authors comment below are, in my opinion, a good summary of the contributions of the paper. While I don't think those contributions are groundbreaking, I believe they are significant enough to merit acceptance. The reason I am commenting here is because, having looked at several comment sections for this ICLR, I am seeing a general trend that reviews have a strong focus on performance, i.e. reviews tend to be very short and judge papers, to a large degree, on whether they are a few percentage points better or worse than the reported baseline. E.g. see the comments "the experimental evaluation is not convincing, e.g. no improvement on SVHN" or "the effect of drop-path seems to vanish with data augmentation" below. I believe that papers should be judged more on their scientific contributions (see points (1), (2) and (4) below), especially when those papers themselves state that their focus is on those scientific contributions, not on amazing performance. Further, I believe the trend to focus excessively on performance is problematic for a number of reasons: - The Deep Learning community has focused very heavily on a few datasets (MNIST, ImageNet, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN). This means that at any time, a large chunk of the deep learning literature is battling for 5 SOTA titles. Hence, expecting any new model to attain one of those titles is a very high bar. - It is an arbitrary standard. Say the SOTA on ImageNet improves by 2% a year. Then a paper that outperforms by 1% in 2014 would underperform by 1% in 2015. By the performance standard, the same paper with the same ideas and the same scientific merit would have declined drastically in value over that one year. Is that really true? - How does one even draw a "fair comparison" on these standard datasets at this point? The bag of tricks for neural networks includes: drop-out, l2, l1, ensembling, various forms of data augmentation, various forms of normalization and initialization, various non-linearities, various learning rate schedules, various forms of pooling, label smoothing, gradient clipping etc. etc. There are a gazillion ways to eke out fractions of percentage points of performance. And - every single paper has a unique combination of tricks that they use for their model, even though the tricks themselves are unrelated to the model. Hence, the only truly fair comparison would be to compare against every reference model with the exact trick combination that the paper presenting the reference model used, which would take an exorbitant amount of time. What's worse, many papers do not even report all of the tricks they used. One would have to get the authors code and reverse engineer the model, not to mention slight differences introduced by using e.g. TensorFlow vs. Torch vs. Caffe. In this light, the request from one of the reviewers to have a baseline "against which the improvements can be clearly demonstrated by making isolated changes" seems unrealistic to me. - The ML community should not make excessive fine-tuning of models mandatory for publication. By requiring models to beat SOTA, we force each author to fine-tune their model ad nauseum, which leads to an arms race. To get a publications, authors would spend ever more time fine-tuning their models. This can not only lead to "training on the test set", but also wastes the time of researcher that could be better spent exploring new ideas. - It gives too much power to bad research. In science, there is always a certain background rate of "bad" results published: either the numbers are outright fake or the experimental protocol was invalid, e.g. someone used the test set as a validation set or someone did an exorbitant number of random reruns and only published the best single result. What's worse, these "bad" results are far more likely to hold the SOTA title at any given time than a "good" result. By requiring new publications to beat SOTA, we give too much power to bad results. - It punishes authors for reporting many or strong baselines. In this paper, authors were careful to report many recent results. Table 1 is thorough. And now they are criticized for not beating all of those baselines. I have a feeling that if the authors of this paper had been more selective about which baselines they report, i.e. those that they can beat, they would have received higher scores on the paper. I have written an in-depth review for another paper at this conference that used, in my opinion, very weak baselines and ended up getting high reviewer marks. I don't think that was a coincidence. The same arguments apply, though I think to a lesser degree, to judging models excessively on how many parameters they have or their runtime. However, I agree with reviewers that more information about how models compare in terms of those metrics would enhance this paper. I would like to see a discussion of that in the final version. In general, I think this paper would benefit from an appendix with more details on model and training procedure. I also agree with reviewers that 80 layers, which is the deepest that authors can go while improving test error (Table 3), is not ultra-deep. Hence putting "ultra-deep" in the paper title seems exaggerated and I would recommend scaling back the language. However, I don't think being ultra-deep (~1000 layers) is necessary, because as Veit et al showed, networks that appear ultra deep might not be ultra deep in practice. Training an 80-layer net that functions at test time without residual connections seems to be enough of an achievement.
sampled: The manuscript, Improving Invariance and Equivariance Properties of Convolutional Neural Networks, addresses an important topic: invariance, equivariance, and equivalence in CNN representations under data augmentation. I appreciate the attempt to study these representation properties across 9 transformation types and to connect empirical measurements with training objectives for Convolutional Neural Networks. The framing is relevant, though the quoted claim that "This is related to the idea of whether CNNs collapse (invariance) or linearize (equivariance) view manifolds of 3D objects" needs correction. The paper’s main contribution appears to be a systematic empirical examination of how data augmentation affects invariance, equivariance, and equivalence, together with proposed extra loss terms intended to make learned representations more invariant or equivariant, but the manuscript should be clearer about what is new relative to prior measurement work by Lenc & Vedaldi. The authors deserve credit for examining data augmentation effects in a systematic way, yet the current presentation does not make sufficiently clear why the observed effects are surprising, interesting, or useful. The abstract’s reference to 9 transformation types is useful context, but the review would benefit from a clearer explanation of whether the findings over these transformations reveal behavior that was not already expected from using data augmentation during training. The manuscript studies a meaningful question, but the motivation and interpretation currently do not establish the practical or conceptual payoff strongly enough. A central concern is that several empirical findings seem expected rather than surprising. If a network is trained with data augmentation, one would expect greater invariance to the augmented transformations. One would also expect identical augmentations to produce more similar representations than different augmentations, so the paper should better explain what conclusions go beyond these intuitions. The proposed losses are another important part of the submission. The paper proposes extra terms for encouraging invariance or equivariance. This direction is plausible. Yet the manuscript does not show substantial performance gains from training for greater invariance or equivariance. That weakens the practical case for the method. The added computational burden also matters. The proposed technique currently seems unlikely to be useful without stronger evidence that the extra training objective improves performance. This concern is especially important for the loss in eq. 6, which is criticized because of its computational cost and because the manuscript does not show that the cost buys substantial gains. If the method mainly changes representation diagnostics without improving task outcomes, that limitation should be stated directly. The paper should separate the value of measuring invariance and equivariance from the value of explicitly optimizing for them, since the evidence appears stronger for the former than for the latter. The manuscript would also be improved by explaining whether increased invariance or equivariance is intended as an end in itself, or only as a means to better performance. At present, the results do not convincingly support the latter. This makes the contribution feel incomplete. Clarify the utility. Show gains. Or qualify the claims. The paper can still be useful as an analysis of data augmentation effects, but the stronger methodological claim requires evidence that the added objective is worth its computational burden. The discussion of equivariance needs more precision. The claim connecting equivariance to linearized manifolds is incorrect as stated. The quoted sentence about whether CNNs collapse or linearize view manifolds of 3D objects should be revised or removed. The manuscript should avoid implying that equivariance itself means that manifolds have been linearized, unless that claim is explicitly defined and supported within the paper’s formalism. The definition associated with eq. 2 also needs correction. The quantity appears better described as non-equivariance rather than equivariance. If the paper defines a deviation from an equivariant prediction, then naming it equivariance may confuse the reader about the direction of the measurement. This issue affects interpretation of the reported diagnostic quantities, not only notation. There is also a concern about the definition of x’_ij. The current formulation may apply a transformation twice rather than undoing it, and the paper should check this carefully. If the intended comparison requires reversing a transformation before comparing representations, the notation should make that explicit. This is particularly important because the central topic is how representations respond to transformations. The manuscript would benefit from clearer mathematical language around eq. 2. The phrase "Eq. 2 also uses the paradigm that" is awkward and should be rewritten. The term paradigm does not seem appropriate there. There is also a typo, "equivaraince". In section 3.3, the formatting of argmax should be corrected. These are local issues, but they affect readability in a paper whose contribution depends on precise definitions. The paper should also ensure that all transformation notation is consistent with the intended invariance or equivariance measurement. The discussion of equivariance could be strengthened by giving a cleaner account of what transformation is represented in the feature space. A 2D rotation matrix example may help only if the manuscript clearly distinguishes the transformation applied to the input from the corresponding transformation expected in the representation. If the quantity in eq. 2 measures failure to match the expected transformed representation, then the text should say non-equivariance. The same care should apply to equivalence and invariance, since the paper compares related but distinct representation properties. Lenc & Vedaldi are relevant prior work here, and the manuscript should make clearer how its measurement framework differs from or extends that earlier work. The strongest part of the paper is the systematic examination of data augmentation effects, not the current evidence for the added loss terms. The weakest part is the gap between representation-property measurements and demonstrated performance benefit. The paper addresses a timely and relevant question for representation learning in computer vision, but its claims should be narrowed unless the authors can show substantial gains from the proposed training terms. I would encourage revisions focused on clearer novelty relative to Lenc & Vedaldi, corrected equivariance definitions around eq. 2, and stronger evidence justifying the cost of eq. 6.

original: Reviewers agree that this paper is based on a "trick" to build memory without requiring long-distance backprop. This method allows the model to utilize a cache-like mechanism, simply by storing previous states. Everyone agrees that this roughly works (although there could be stronger experimental evidence), and provides long-term memory to simple models. Reviewers/authors also agree that it might not work as well as other pointer-network like method, but there is controversy over whether that is necessary. - Further discussion indicated a sense by some reviewers that this method could be quite impactful, even if it was not a huge technical contribution, due to its speed and computational benefits over pointer methods. - The clarity of the writing and good use of references was appreciated - This paper is a nice complement/rebuttal to "Frustratingly Short Attention Spans in Neural Language Modeling". Including the discussion about this paper as it might be helpful as it was controversial: """ The technical contribution may appear "limited" but I feel part of that is necessary to ensure the method can scale to both large datasets and long term dependencies. For me, this is similar to simpler machine learning methods being able to scale to more data (though replacing "data" with "timesteps"). More complex methods may do better with a small number of data/timesteps but they won't be able to scale, where other specific advantages may come in to play. (Timesteps) Looking back 2000 timesteps is something I've not seen done and speaks to a broader aspect of language modeling - properly capturing recent article level context. Most language models limit BPTT to around 35 timesteps, with some even arguing we don't need that much (i.e. "Frustratingly Short Attention Spans in Neural Language Modeling" that's under review for ICLR). From a general perspective, this is vaguely mad given many sentences are longer than 35 timesteps, yet we know both intuitively and from the evidence they present that the rest of an article is very likely to help modeling the following words, especially for PTB or WikiText. This paper introduces a technique that not only allows for utilizing dependencies far further back than 35 timesteps but shows it consistently helps, even when thrown against a larger number of timesteps, a larger dataset, or a larger vocabulary. Given it is also a post-processing step that can be applied to any vaguely RNN type model, it's widely applicable and trivial to train in comparison to any more complicated models. (Data) Speaking to AnonReviewer1's comment, "A side-by-side comparison of models with pointer networks vs. models with cache with roughly the same number of parameters is needed to convincingly argue that the proposed method is a better alternative (either because it achieves lower perplexity, faster to train but similar test perplexity, faster at test time, etc.)" Existing pointer network approaches for language modeling are very slow to train - or at least more optimal methods are yet to be discovered - and has such limited the BPTT length they tackle. Merity et al. use 100 at most and that's the only pointer method for language modeling attending to article style text that I am aware of. Merity et al. also have a section of their paper specifically discussing the training speed complications that come from integrating the pointer network. There is a comparison to Merity et al. in Table 1 and Table 2. The scaling becomes more obvious on the WikiText datasets which have a more realistic long tail vocabulary than PTB's 10k. For WikiText-2, at a cache size of 100, Merity et al. get 80.8 with their pointer network method while the neural cache model get 81.6. Increasing the neural model cache size to 2000 however gives quite a substantial drop to 68.9. They're also able to apply their method to WikiText-103, a far larger dataset than PTB or WikiText-2, and show that it still provides improvements even when there is more data and a larger vocabulary.
sampled: The paper Knowledge as a Teacher: Knowledge-Guided Structural Attention Networks addresses natural language understanding through sequence tagging and slot filling. I understand the main contribution as a method to "flatten" structured information into memory vectors, which then provide extra context to a tagger. The proposed K-SAN architecture is simple and practical, and the paper presents a clear motivation for using structural attention with RNN models. I am less convinced that the architecture is fully novel, but the idea of converting sentence structure and substructure information into usable contextual vectors is still potentially useful. The proposed model has two main parts, sentence embedding and substructure embedding, and this organization makes the method easy to follow at a high level, especially for readers interested in how syntax can be represented for sequence tagging. The evaluation on ATIS appears positive, but the experimental evidence is not yet persuasive enough. My main concern is that the baseline descriptions in Table 1 are insufficient, especially for TreeRNN and DCNN. The paper should explain more clearly how TreeRNN and DCNN are applied to sentence and substructure embeddings. The comparison to baselines is difficult to assess because the proposed model uses two RNNs, which may give it greater parameter capacity than the competing systems. This issue matters because a gain over TreeRNN or DCNN could reflect model size rather than the proposed use of structural attention. The paper should report neural network hyperparameters for the baselines and provide comparable parameter counts so that the empirical claims can be interpreted more reliably. Major concern. A stronger baseline would provide the extra knowledge directly as RNN input features, rather than using the proposed memory and attention mechanism. This would help show whether K-SAN improves because of the structural attention design or because the model simply receives additional syntactic information. The relevant comparison could use the knowledge vector as part of the RNN input, as suggested by Eqn 5 and 8. Such a baseline is important because the paper claims benefits from knowledge-guided structural attention, but without this comparison the contribution of the attention mechanism remains under-specified, and a direct feature-based RNN could be a competitive and simpler alternative. The use of one static attention distribution also needs more justification, since a word-specific attention distribution over substructures seems natural for a slot filling task where different words may require different structural cues. The current similarity-based weighting may favor nodes or phrases that are similar to the full sentence, rather than those most useful for individual tag decisions. Clarify sensitivity. The paper should discuss whether K-SAN is sensitive to parser mistakes, because the model depends on syntax-derived information and the empirical evidence covers one dataset, so it is hard to know whether the results reflect robust use of structure or successful use of relatively clean structural inputs in this setting. The related work discussion should be tightened around DCNN and related substructure encoders, including Ma et al., Zhao et al, Liu et al., and Eriguchi et al. The current framing leaves uncertainty about which parts of K-SAN differ from these prior uses of structured or hierarchical representations. It would also help to explain why the syntax information is called "knowledge" and whether that term is meant to include other forms such as AMR or NER. Without that clarification, the claimed generality to different forms of knowledge is not fully supported. After rebuttal, my main concerns about baselines and the two-RNN design remain unresolved. The response does not adequately establish that the improvements come from the proposed structural attention mechanism rather than from additional parameters or added input information. The paper is promising as a practical model for incorporating syntax into sequence tagging, but its empirical support needs stronger controls. I would encourage the authors to revise the experimental section so that TreeRNN, DCNN, and feature-based RNN comparisons are described with enough detail for fair interpretation. At present, the work is understandable and potentially useful, but the evidence does not yet justify the strength of the claims about novelty, generality, and effectiveness.

original: This paper proposes a generative model of videos composed of a background and a set of 2D objects (sprites). Optimization is performed under a VAE framework. The authors' proposal of an outer product of softmaxed vectors (resulting in a 2D map that is delta-like), composed with a convolution, is a very interesting way to achieve translation of an image with differentiable parameters. It seems to be an attractive alternative to more complicated differentiable resamplers (such as those used by STNs) when only translation is needed. Below I have made some comments regarding parts of the text, especially the experiments, that are not clear. The experimental section in particular seems rushed, with some results only alluded to but not given, not even in the appendix. For an extremely novel and exotic proposal, showing only synthetic experiments could be excused. However, though there is some novelty in the method, it is disappointing that there isn't even an attempt at trying to tackle a problem with real data. I suggest as an example aerial videos (such as those taken from drone platforms), since the planar assumption that the authors make would most probably hold in that case. I also suggest that the authors do another pass at proof-reading the paper. There are missing references ("Fig. ??"), unfinished sentences (caption of Fig. 5), and the aforementioned issues with the experimental exposition.
sampled: Program Synthesis for Character Level Language Modeling presents a novel language modeling method for both programming and natural language, and the paper has clear appeal as a 1: novel approach. The central idea is distinctive among the comparisons discussed. The method searches a program space using program synthesis, estimates program weights using counts, and contrasts with neural network methods that use gradient descent and are slow to estimate. Ordinary n-gram models are framed as limited by simplicity, weak large-context modeling, and poor scaling as context grows, while the proposed MCMC-synthesized programs can learn context-sensitive probabilities while keeping count-based speed. The empirical results are a major strength, especially on the linux kernel corpus, where the approach is reported as much stronger than LSTM and n-gram language models. On the Wikipedia corpus, the method is described as competitive with state-of-the-art models, though it does not surpass them, which makes the natural language evidence positive but more qualified. The efficiency claims are also important, since estimation and query times are reported as much better than LSTM language models and comparable with n-gram language models. This helps distinguish the contribution from both neural network baselines and ordinary count-based baselines, and it supports the claim that the method combines context-sensitive modeling with count-based speed.

original: The paper presents a clean framework for optimizing for the network size during the training cycle. While the complexity of each iteration is increased, they argue that overall, the cost is significantly reduced since we do not need to train networks of varying sizes and cross-validate across them. The reviewers recommend acceptance of the paper and I am in agreement with them.

original: This paper not only shows that a cache model on top of a pre-trained RNN can improve language modeling, but also illustrates a shortcoming of standard RNN models in that they are unable to capture this information themselves. Regardless of whether this is due to the small BPTT window (35 is standard) or an issue with the capability of the RNN itself, this is a useful insight. This technique is an interesting variation of memory augmented neural networks with a number of advantages to many of the standard memory augmented architectures. They illustrate the neural cache model on not just the Penn Treebank but also WikiText-2 and WikiText-103, two datasets specifically tailored to illustrating long term dependencies with a more realistic vocabulary size. I have not seen the ability to refer up to 2000 words back previously. I recommend this paper be accepted. There is additionally extensive analysis of the hyperparameters on these datasets, providing further insight. I recommend this interesting and well analyzed paper be accepted.
sampled: The paper BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION BY HIERARCHICAL DIRICHLET PROCESS HIDDEN MARKOV MODEL addresses an interesting problem, proposing unsupervised segmentation for bioacoustic data using Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Hidden Markov Models. The submission frames segmentation as difficult because experts lack agreement on appropriate segment boundaries, and it cites Kershenbaum et al. (2014) as motivation for understanding animal behavior. The main novelty appears to be the application of an existing HDP-HMM approach to bioacoustic segmentation, rather than the introduction of a new model. The empirical case is not convincing, because the method often does not match segmentations defined by human experts, even though human expert annotations are treated as the evaluation baseline. Two real sound-scene applications are investigated, whale and multi-species bird segmentation. Model learning uses MCMC on MFCC representations of audio signals. These choices are appropriate to describe, but the evidence presented does not establish that the Bayesian non-parametric sequential model provides reliable segmentation for the stated bioacoustic tasks.

original: This paper is clearly written, and contains original observations on the properties of the neural GPU model. These observations are an important part of research, and sharing them (and code) will help the field move forward. However, these observations do not quite add up to a coherent story, nor is a particular set of hypotheses explored in depth. So the main problem with this paper is that it doesn't fit the 'one main idea' standard format of papers, making it hard to build on this work. The other big problem with this paper is the lack of comparison to similar architectures. There is lots of intuition given about why the NGPU should work better than other architectures in some situations, but not much empirical validation of this idea.
sampled: Recurrent Batch Normalization is a useful contribution because it successfully adapts batch normalization for RNNs, where prior use had failed or performed poorly. The experiments show clear gains of batch-normalized LSTMs over standard LSTMs, and the evaluation spans character-level, word-level, and pixel-level examples. The coverage across PTB, Text8, the CNN question-answering task, MNIST, and pMNIST gives the assessment a broad basis within sequence modeling and recurrent settings. I also appreciated the discussion of gradient flow, especially the role of unit variance in tanh derivatives, and found the Figure 1b "toy task" demonstration useful for supporting the stated gradient-flow insight. The pMNIST experiment is a meaningful part of the evidence because it suggests that batch normalization helps recurrent models learn long-term dependencies.

original: The paper presents the semantic embedding model for multi-label prediction. In my questions, I pointed that the proposed approach assumes the number of labels to predict is known, and the authors said this was an orthogonal question, although I don't think it is! I was trying to understand how different is SEM from a basic MLP with softmax output which would be trained with a two step approach instead of stochastic gradient descent. sampled: The paper presents Generative Matching Networks as a VAE-based method for conditional sample generation. The approach is clear in its use of a recurrent neural network plus aggregation to process an exemplar set, with an aggregation mechanism resembling Matching Networks and producing an exemplar representation that conditions the VAE generator for generating samples of a concept from several provided exemplars. The conditioning and aggregation are a strength because they are described as handling exemplar sets drawn from multiple classes better than simple averaging, and the experiments show generalization from conditioning on 2 classes to conditioning on 4 classes. The use of OMNIGLOT is appropriate for assessing one-shot conditional generation, and the experiments are quite convincing.

original: This paper addresses one of the major shortcomings of generative adversarial networks - their lack of mechanism for evaluating held-out data. While other work such as BiGANs/ALI address this by learning a separate inference network, here the authors propose to change the GAN objective function such that the optimal discriminator is also an energy function, rather than becoming uninformative at the optimal solution. Training this new objective requires gradients of the entropy of the generated data, which are difficult to approximate, and the authors propose two methods to do so, one based on nearest neighbors and one based on a variational lower bound. The results presented show that on toy data the learned discriminator/energy function closely approximates the log probability of the data, and on more complex data the discriminator give a good measure of quality for held out data. I would say the largest shortcomings of the paper are practical issues around the scalability of the nearest neighbors approximation and accuracy of the variational approximation, which the authors acknowledge. Also, since entropy estimation and density estimation are such closely linked problems, I wonder if any practical method for EGANs will end up being equivalent to some form of approximate density estimation, exactly the problem GANs were designed to circumvent. Nonetheless, the elegant mathematical exposition alone makes the paper a worthwhile contribution to the literature. Also, some quibbles about the writing - it seems that something is missing in the sentence at the top of pg. 5 "Finally, let's whose discriminative power". I'm not sure what the authors mean to say here.
sampled: The Neural Noisy Channel proposes using an SSNT model for p(x|y) in a noisy channel approach to conditional generation, while still supporting incremental generation of y. The paper also introduces an approximate decoding search method, and the reviewer finds the empirical evaluation extensive and strong, with good empirical results that make the proposed approach a substantive contribution rather than only a modeling variation. The SSNT model is interesting and appropriately motivated for this application, since the formulation directly addresses the role of p(x|y) in conditional generation and gives the paper a clear modeling rationale. The paper is generally clear and well written, and its combination of a noisy channel formulation, sequence-to-sequence transduction, beam search decoding, and empirical evaluation is presented in a way that is accessible and technically focused. The main concern is whether the extra training and decoding cost is justified by the gains, since a simpler alternative might capture some of the same benefits without the same modeling and search burden. In particular, reranking complete outputs from a standard seq2seq model using p(y|x), p(x|y), and p(y) might provide similar gains, and Li et al. at NAACL 2016 are relevant here as a comparison point for reranking in conversation modeling. Experiments on reranking during search would be useful for clarifying this issue and strengthening the empirical case. Section 2 could also be presented more consistently from the viewpoint of modeling p(x|y), since that perspective appears central to the proposed approach. This would improve focus. The discussion of "explaining away" is relevant to the noisy channel motivation. Clarifying how the model addresses that issue, while separating it from the cost question, would make the paper’s claims easier to assess and would better connect the modeling motivation with the empirical results.

original: - Strengths: * Elaborate evaluation data creation and evaluation scheme. * Range of compared techniques: baseline/simple/complex - Weaknesses: * No in-depth analysis beyond overall evaluation results. - General Discussion: This paper compares several techniques for robust HPSG parsing. Since the main contribution of the paper is not a novel parsing technique but the empirical evaluation, I would like to see a more in-depth analysis of the results summarized in Table 1 and 2. It would be nice to show some representative example sentences and sketches of its analyses, on which the compared methods behaved differently. Please add EDM precision and recall figures to Table 2. The EDM F1 score is a result of a mixed effects of (overall and partial) coverage, parse ranking, efficiency of search, etc. The overall coverage figures in Table 1 are helpful but addition of EDM recall to Table 2 would make the situations clearer. sampled: This is a strong submission with useful theoretical contributions, especially in connecting value-based reinforcement learning with policy-gradient approaches. The proposed PGQL method is clearly positioned between policy gradient and Q-learning. A central strength is the formal relationship between Q-values and regularized policy gradient policies. I suggest presenting PGQL more explicitly as an extension or generalization of the dueling Q-network, since that framing seems more intuitive for explaining both the algorithm and the reported findings. This comparison would also help readers understand how the value and policy components relate to existing Q-learning architectures. My main concern is the general-case derivation in Section 3.2. In Eq. (7), the expectation over state-action pairs is taken with respect to pi, while pi depends on theta, and this theta-dependence appears to be ignored. That dependency seems important for deriving the policy-gradient update, so the current step may optimize a different objective than intended.

original: Thank you to all the reviewers for their comments. We believe that these are the primary points raised by the reviewers: 1. A comparison with a neural programming technique which does not generate code would be a valuable addition to our experiments. We did not include a comparison to a network which does not generate source code because because they usually require substantially more training data than the 5 input-output examples we provide to have any success at generalization. While it would be interesting to show this effect in experiments, the wide variety of different models and training strategies, the custom structure of list data and list-aware objective function in our work, together with the lack of released standard implementations, makes it unclear what neural programming baseline (and with what training regime) would be appropriate. 2. The tasks our network can learn are simple. In particular, we do not consider sorting or merging problems. Although the tasks that we considered are simple, they are more complex than the tasks which many other neural programming approaches can handle, particularly as we test for perfect generalization. The approaches to learning to sort do so using program traces, which provide much stronger supervision than the input-output examples that we use [1], or use specialized memory representations that simplify sorting [2]. 3. This paper does not conclusively show that gradient-based evaluators are appropriate for program induction. This paper certainly does not contradict the findings of the original TerpreT paper that discrete solvers are good backends for program induction. Our motivation in this paper is to improve gradient-based program search, and to understand the effect of different design choices that arise when building differentiable interpreters. Even if gradient descent isn't currently the best method for program induction, we believe it merits further study. It is a very new idea, and it's feasible to us that seemingly subtle design decisions could make a big difference in its performance (indeed, this is one take-away from our experiments). Further, since gradient descent is very different from alternatives, improving its performance may enable new uses of program synthesis such as jointly inducing programs and training neural network subcomponents as in [3], using SGD to scale up to large data sets, or giving new ways of thinking about noisy data in program synthesis. Finally, the recommendations for the design of such evaluators discussed in this paper are not necessarily restricted to TerpreT-based models, and we believe that our design recommendations apply to related neural architectures that try to learn algorithmic patterns. 4. How will this model generalize to programs that can't be solved using the prefix-loop-suffix structure? Defining new program structures is simple, and our current implementation allows the optimizer to choose between several program structures. More loops could be added if desired, and more looping schemes could be added to extend the class of programs which can be learned. 5. TerpreT is not yet publicly available. TerpreT is nearly ready for public release. Approval for open-sourcing under the MIT license has been obtained, and we are currently in the process of documenting the source code to publish it (with all models used in this paper). References: [1] Scott Reed and Nando de Freitas. Neural Programmer-Interpreters. In ICLR 2016. [2] Marcin Andrychowicz, Karol Kurach. Learning Efficient Algorithms with Hierarchical Attentive Memory.
sampled: The paper presents an interesting contribution on spatiotemporal visual attention. I consider the work accepted, while noting several points that should be clarified. The contribution is clear. Recurrent Mixture Density Network for Spatiotemporal Visual Attention proposes a recurrent neural model for predicting human video fixations. The formulation is appealing because it predicts human video fixations through a Gaussian mixture formulation and trains the model by maximum likelihood using human fixation data, which gives the approach a direct connection to the observed fixation distribution rather than only to derived saliency maps. The evaluation also has useful breadth, since the work studies fixation prediction on Hollywood2 and tests generalization and action classification on UCF101, while also using saliency outputs with C3D features for action recognition, but the presentation would benefit from a more complete assessment of fixation prediction quality. The experimental framing raises questions. Table 1 and Table 2 appear to report substantially different center bias results. This difference should be explained because it affects how the proposed model is interpreted. Central Bias is an important reference point here, and the paper should describe more fully how that baseline was modeled and how it relates to the human performance comparison. The claim that the model results are within 3.2% of human performance should be handled carefully, because comparing gaps in AUC scores can be risky when saturation effects may make differences hard to interpret. Human performance needs clarification. Was the human performance estimate cross-validated, or was it computed in another way? The comparison with state-of-the-art methods is not fully convincing in its current form. In particular, I am not sure whether all models in Table 2 are truly worse than the center bias result reported in Table 1. If that is the intended conclusion, the paper should make the evaluation setup and the center bias computation directly comparable across the two tables. If it is not the intended conclusion, the table presentation should prevent that reading. The current presentation leaves open whether the apparent difference reflects evaluation details, dataset handling, or the way the baseline was defined. The authors should also explain how the human performance estimate fits into the same comparison, since it is used as an upper reference for the proposed model and for the claimed small remaining gap. The discussion of Kümmerer et. al 2015 also appears inaccurate, because that model was trained on fixation data with maximum likelihood, whereas the paper describes it as a method that "learns ... indirectly rather than from explicit information of where humans look". This citation issue matters. It affects the positioning of the proposed maximum likelihood training objective relative to prior fixation-based saliency models. Table 3 is confusing in its explanation, especially in the distinction between how CONV5 and FC6 use the saliency map. The authors should clarify why these layers use the saliency information differently and what comparison Table 3 is meant to support. The action recognition experiment is a useful component because it connects saliency prediction to C3D features. The paper should make the role of the predicted saliency outputs in that experiment easier to follow. The broader evaluation would be stronger if fixation prediction quality were assessed more completely before using the saliency outputs in action recognition.

original: - Strengths: This paper proposed an interesting and important metric for evaluating the quality of word embeddings, which is the "data efficiency" when it is used in other supervised tasks. Another interesting point in the paper is that the authors separated out three questions: 1) whether supervised task offers more insights to evaluate embedding quality; 2) How stable is the ranking vs labeled data set size; 3) The benefit to linear vs non-linear models. Overall, the authors presented comprehensive experiments to answer those questions, and the results see quite interesting to know for the research community. - Weaknesses: The overall result is not very useful for ML practioners in this field, because it merely confirms what has been known or suspected, i.e. it depends on the task at hand, the labeled data set size, the type of the model, etc. So, the result in this paper is not very actionable. The reviewer noted that this comprehensive analysis deepens the understanding of this topic. - General Discussion: The paper's presentation can be improved. Specifically: 1) The order of the figures/tables in the paper should match the order they are mentioned in the papers. Right now their order seems quite random. 2) Several typos (L250, 579, etc). Please use a spell checker. 3) Equation 1 is not very useful, and its exposition looks strange. It can be removed, and leave just the text explanations. 4) L164 mentions the "Appendix", but it is not available in the paper. 5) Missing citation for the public skip-gram data set in L425. 6) The claim in L591-593 is too strong. It must be explained more clearly, i.e. when it is useful and when it is not. 7) The observation in L642-645 is very interesting and important. It will be good to follow up on this and provide concrete evidence or example from some embedding. Some visualization may help too. 8) In L672 should provide examples of such "specialized word embeddings" and how they are different than the general purpose embedding. 9) Figuer 3 is too small to read.
sampled: The paper addresses a genuine need in the field, as qualitative sample inspection remains a common evaluation practice for models such as Generative Adversarial Networks and Generative Moment Matching Networks, and a principled quantitative alternative has real value. The central contribution is a framework that uses Annealed Importance Sampling to estimate log-likelihoods for decoder-based generative models, validates those estimates through Bidirectional Monte Carlo, and demonstrates on binarized MNIST that this approach is more accurate than Kernel Density Estimation across Variational Autoencoders, Importance Weighted Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks, and Generative Moment Matching Networks. The finding that the Importance Weighted Autoencoder bound underestimates true log-likelihoods by at least 1 nat on binarized MNIST is a concrete and useful result. Making the evaluation framework public is a meaningful contribution given the persistent difficulty of reproducibility in generative model evaluation; the authors also disconfirm the hypothesis that Generative Adversarial Networks memorize training data, showing instead that these models miss important modes of the data distribution, which is a substantive empirical finding. Several concerns remain. The chain count is low: prior work by Salakhutdinov and Murray, 2008 and Desjardins et al., 2011 used 100 chains, yet this paper uses only 16 independent AIS chains with no justification given. The experiments also draw varying numbers of examples—100, 1000, and 10000—from different data sources without explanation of why a consistent setup was not used, which complicates direct comparison. GAN50 shows a Bidirectional Monte Carlo gap of 10 nats, roughly an order of magnitude larger than the gaps observed for other models, yet the authors offer no intuition for why this occurs; given its scale relative to the other evaluated models, this gap warrants explicit discussion. Finally, Table 1 is not referenced anywhere in the main text and its columns are not described, and the caption of Figure 3 contains a labeling error.

original: The paper explores a simple approach to learning reward functions for reinforcement learning from visual observations of expert trajectories for cases were only little training data is available. To obtain descriptive rewards even under such challenging conditions the method re-uses a pre-trained neural network as feature extractor (this is similar to a large body of work on task transfer with neural nets in the area of computer vision) and represents the reward function as a weighted distance to features for automatically extracted "key-frames" of the provided expert trajectories. The paper is well written and explains all involved concepts clearly while also embedding the presented approach in the literature on inverse reinforcement learning (IRL). The resulting algorithm is appealing due to its simplicity and could prove useful for many real world robotic applications. I have three main issues with the paper in its current form, if these can be addressed I believe the paper would be significantly strengthened: 1) Although the recursive splitting approach for extracting the "key-frames" seems reasonable and the feature selection is well motivated I am missing two baselines in the experiments: - what happens if the feature selection is disabled and the distance between all features is used ? will this immediately break the procedure ? If not, what is the trade-off here ? - an even simpler baseline than what is proposed in the paper would be the following procedure: simply use all frames of the recorded trajectories, calculate the distance to them in feature space and weights them according to their time as in the approach proposed in the paper. How well would that work ? 2) I understand the desire to combine the extracted reward function with a simple RL method but believe the used simple controller could potentially introduce a significant bias in the experiments since it requires initialization from an expert trajectory. As a direct consequence of this initialization the RL procedure is already started close to a good solution and the extracted reward function is potentially only queried in a small region around what was observed in the initial set of images (perhaps with the exception of the human demonstrations). Without an additional experiment it is thus unclear how well the presented approach will work in combination with other RL methods for training the controller. 3) I understand that the low number of available images excludes training a deep neural net directly for the task at hand but one has to wonder how other baselines would do. What happens if one uses a random projection of the images to form a feature vector? How well would a distance measure using raw images (e.g. L2 norm of image differences) or a distance measure based on the first principal components work? It seems that occlusions etc. would exclude them from working well but without empirical evidence it is hard to confirm this. Minor issues: - Page 1: "make use of ideas about imitation" reads a bit awkwardly - Page 3: "We use the Inception network pre-trained ImageNet" -> pre-trained for ImageNet classification - Page 4: the definition of the transition function for the stochastic case seems broken - Page 6: "efficient enough to evaluate" a bit strangely written sentence Additional comments rather than real issues: - The paper is mainly of empirical nature, little actual learning is performed to obtain the reward function and no theoretical advances are needed. sampled: This paper on Probabilistic Regular Graph Languages is formally correct, clearly written, and makes a genuine contribution to the formal language theory underlying natural language processing. Researchers working on graph-based semantic parsing are likely to find the ideas stimulating. The central results—that Regular Graph Languages are closed under intersection and that a parsing algorithm with runtime linear in the size of the input graph can be constructed—are well-established within the paper, though their practical interpretation for NLP applications needs more careful framing than the current draft provides. The most pressing concern is that the paper does not adequately distinguish between semantic parsing from strings and the parsing or validation of semantic parses already in graph form. The linear complexity result applies to top-down deterministic grammars and is properly understood as a graph validation result, not as a claim about recovering semantic parses from raw string input. This distinction matters: an input string in NLP typically gives rise to an exponential number of graphs, a fact the paper does not acknowledge and which substantially limits the directness of the claimed NLP applicability. The algorithm is well-suited to reranking hypergraphs produced by a separate parser—a genuinely useful role in NLP pipelines—but this reranking use case is absent from the introduction, leaving readers to infer a more direct parsing role than the formalism supports. Extending the parser to handle string inputs would require tracking covered 0-arity edges, and this variant becomes exponential rather than linear. It is also unclear whether the Earley recogniser remains strictly polynomial in m or k when grammars are ambiguous or not top-down deterministic, and this case is not addressed. A further gap is the absence of any clear connection to non-context-free string languages or to the sets of non-projective dependency graphs that appear in practical semantic parsing contexts, including AMR. The remark at lines 644–647 touches on a related point but arrives too late and would benefit readers if moved earlier. A discussion of Monadic Second Order graph languages and their yields—context-free string languages in the sense explored by Courcelle, Kuhlmann, and Jonsson—would help situate the contribution more precisely within the existing literature. Several specific passages also need attention. Lines 102–106 are misleading in their treatment of intersection and probabilities. Line 173 uses the word "parsing" where "validation" or "recognition" would be more precise. Lines 195–196 are unclear regarding the elements of att_G. Line 352 would benefit from an example of a nontrivial internal path. Lines 757–758 are misleading on the claim that HRGs generate non-context-free languages, and line 760 invites scrutiny on the assertion about non-crossing links when parsing linearized sentences. The paper demands close reading and substantial formal background from its audience. While it is admirably precise given that background, the authors should consider revising the introduction to set more accurate expectations about the relationship between the graph-theoretic results and the practical constraints of string-to-graph semantic parsing tasks such as those involving AMR. Addressing the distinction between graph validation and string-to-graph parsing consistently throughout—particularly in the introduction and wherever NLP applicability is claimed—would strengthen the work considerably.

original: - Strengths: Detailed guidelines and explicit illustrations. - Weaknesses: The document-independent crowdsourcing annotation is unreliable. - General Discussion: This work creates a new benchmark corpus for concept-map-based MDS. It is well organized and written clearly. The supplement materials are sufficient. I have two questions here. 1) Is it necessary to treat concept map extraction as a separate task? On the one hand, many generic summarization systems build a similar knowledge graph and then generate summaries accordingly. On the other hand, with the increase of the node number, the concept map becomes growing hard to distinguish. Thus, the general summaries should be more readable. 2) How can you determine the importance of a concept independent of the documents? The definition of summarization is to reserve the main concepts of documents. Therefore, the importance of a concept highly depends on the documents. For example, in the given topic of coal mining accidents, assume there are two concepts: A) an instance of coal mining accidents and B) a cause of coal mining accidents. Then, if the document describes a series of coal mining accidents, A is more important than B. In comparison, if the document explores why coal mining accidents happen, B is more significant than A. Therefore, just given the topic and two concepts A&B, it is impossible to judge their relative importance. I appreciate the great effort spent by authors to build this dataset. However, this dataset is more like a knowledge graph based on common sense rather than summary.
sampled: The main novelty here is the use of marginal Fisher analysis as a new layer in a deep architecture. That said, several concerns remain. Similar ideas appeared in prior work roughly 3 to 5 years ago, with SPCANet as one example, which limits the originality of the contribution. The proposed MDA method combines MFA initialization with existing components—greedy-layerwise stacking, dropout, and denoising auto-encoders—and this combination constrains the claim of novelty. The paper includes a large number of experiments across 7 small to mid-scale datasets, which is appreciated, though the small scale of those datasets is a limitation. The use of back propagation with dropout during fine-tuning is not itself novel. A notable missing comparison is a discriminatively trained convolutional network on CIFAR-10, which would serve as a meaningful baseline. The authors should also demonstrate that MFA initialization outperforms random weight initialization, as this comparison is absent. It is also unclear how computationally expensive it is to compute the association matrix A in equation 4, and the paper does not address this. A convolutional or fully connected network trained from scratch with a good initialization scheme should be included as a baseline so that the benefit of MFA-based initialization can be properly isolated. Without this, it is difficult to attribute observed performance gains to MFA initialization rather than to other components of the pipeline.

original: This paper introduces an energy-based Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) and provides theoretical and empirical results modeling a number of image datasets (including large-scale versions of categories of ImageNet). As far as I know energy-based GANs (EBGAN) were introduced in Kim and Bengio (2016), but the proposed version makes a number of different design choices. First, it does away with the entropy regularization term that Kim and Bengio (2016) introduced to ensure that the GAN discriminator converged to an energy function proportional to the log density of the data (at optimum). This implies that the discriminator in the proposed scheme will become uniform at convergence as discussed in the theoretical section of the paper, however the introductory text seems to imply otherwise -- that one could recover a meaningful score function from the trained energy-function (discriminator). This should be clarified. Second, this version of the EBGAN setting includes two innovations: (1) the introduction of the hinge loss in the value function, and (2) the use of an auto-encoder parametrization for the energy function. These innovations are not empirically justified in any way - this is disappointing, as it would be really good to see empirical results supporting the arguments made in support of their introduction. The two significant contributions of this paper are the theoretical analysis of the energy-baesd GAN formalism (showing that the optimum corresponds to a Nash equilibrium) and the impressive empirical results on large images that set a new standard in what straight GAN-style models can achieve. The theoretical results seem solid to me and make a nice contribution. Regarding the quantitative results in Table 2, it seems not appropriate to bold the EBGAN line when it seems to be statistically indistinguishable form the Rasmus et al (2015) results. Though it is not mentioned here, the use of bold typically indicates the state-of-the-art. I think this paper could be be much stronger if the two novel contributions to the energy-based GAN setting were more thoroughly explored with ablation experiments.
sampled: The paper proposes predicting binary codes to reduce output layer computation to a cost that scales logarithmically in vocabulary size, a well-motivated objective for neural machine translation with large vocabularies. The writing is clear throughout and the figures are well designed, making the technical content accessible. The central result on the E2J task is notable: using 44 bits, the model achieves 26 out of 31 BLEU relative to the softmax baseline, a smaller gap than one might expect given the significant reduction in output layer complexity. On the ASPEC dataset, however, the best proposed model remains 1 BLEU point below the softmax baseline, and it is unclear whether this gap would widen on larger datasets such as the French-English corpus suggested for comparison, which contains up to 12 million sentences. Evaluating on additional language pairs beyond English-Japanese would help clarify how broadly the method generalizes. The paper positions the parameter reduction technique as orthogonal to weight pruning and sequence-level knowledge distillation, which situates it well within the broader efficient NMT literature, and the claim that the method extends to any task with a large output vocabulary strengthens its potential impact. That said, the hidden dimension size of the models is not reported in the experimental setup, making it difficult to fully assess the computational comparisons. It would also be straightforward to ablate the number of bits beyond 44, since the bottleneck lies elsewhere and additional bits could improve classification power without affecting GPU computation time. A related paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.00072 reports a 10x decoding speedup with less than 0.5 BLEU loss and should be cited given its direct relevance; situating the proposed method against that result would sharpen the contribution. Finally, binary code prediction effectively predicts word rank, and the semantic interpretation of individual bit-embeddings under that framing is not clearly established. Clarifying whether the bit structure encodes anything beyond frequency rank would strengthen the paper's interpretive claims.

original: This paper addresses the problem of disambiguating/linking textual entity mentions into a given background knowledge base (in this case, English Wikipedia). (Its title and introduction are a little overblown/misleading, since there is a lot more to bridging text and knowledge than the EDL task, but EDL is a core part of the overall task nonetheless.) The method is to perform this bridging via an intermediate layer of representation, namely mention senses, thus following two steps: (1) mention to mention sense, and (2) mention sense to entity. Various embedding representations are learned for the words, the mention senses, and the entities, which are then jointly trained to maximize a single overall objective function that maximizes all three types of embedding equally. Technically the approach is fairly clear and conforms to the current deep processing fashion and known best practices regarding embeddings; while one can suggest all kinds of alternatives, it’s not clear they would make a material difference. Rather, my comments focus on the basic approach. It is not explained, however, exactly why a two-step process, involving the mention senses, is better than a simple direct one-step mapping from word mentions to their entities. (This is the approach of Yamada et al., in what is called here the ALIGN algorithm.) Table 2 shows that the two-step MPME (and even its simplification SPME) do better. By why, exactly? What is the exact difference, and additional information, that the mention senses have compare4ed to the entities? To understand, please check if the following is correct (and perhaps update the paper to make it exactly clear what is going on). For entities: their profiles consist of neighboring entities in a relatedness graph. This graph is built (I assume) by looking at word-level relatedness of the entity definitions (pages in Wikipedia). The profiles are (extended skip-gram-based) embeddings. For words: their profiles are the standard distributional semantics approach, without sense disambiguation. For mention senses: their profiles are the standard distributional semantics approach, but WITH sense disambiguation. Sense disambiguation is performed using a sense-based profile (‘language model’) from local context words and neighboring mentions, as mentioned briefly just before Section 4, but without details. This is a problem point in the approach. How exactly are the senses created and differentiated? Who defines how many senses a mention string can have? If this is done by looking at the knowledge base, then we get a bijective mapping between mention senses and entities -– that is, there is exactly one entity for each mention sense (even if there may be more entities). In that case, are the sense collection’s definitional profiles built starting with entity text as ‘seed words’? If so, what information is used at the mention sense level that is NOT used at the entity level? Just and exactly the words in the texts that reliably associate with the mention sense, but that do NOT occur in the equivalent entity webpage in Wikipedia? How many such words are there, on average, for a mention sense? That is, how powerful/necessary is it to keep this extra differentiation information in a separate space (the mention sense space) as opposed to just loading these additional words into the Entity space (by adding these words into the Wikipedia entity pages)? If the above understanding is essentially correct, please update Section 5 of the paper to say so, for (to me) it is the main new information in the paper. It is not true, as the paper says in Section 6, that “…this is the first work to deal with mention ambiguity in the integration of text and knowledge representations, so there is no exact baselines for comparison”. The TAC KBP evaluations for the past two years have hosted EDL tasks, involving eight or nine systems, all performing exactly this task, albeit against Freebase, which is considerably larger and more noisy than Wikipedia. Please see http://nlp.cs.rpi.edu/kbp/2016/ . On a positive note: I really liked the idea of the smoothing parameter in Section 6.4.2. Post-response: I have read the authors' responses.
sampled: This paper addresses technically demanding problems in model-based reinforcement learning, and the authors have responded to reviewer concerns by adding new results and discussion, with modifications highlighted in red, primarily in the Appendix. The scope of the revision is substantial, and several structural decisions made in response to criticism deserve careful scrutiny. The authors compare 8 alternative architectures for incorporating actions against the main model, with results in Section B.1.3, Figures 19 and 20, covering 10 Atari games. Combining the action with the frame directly, as in ConvA, is identified as a poor approach, while other direct action influence methods show broadly similar performance to one another. Direct action influence outperforms indirect action influence (as in Oh et al.) in games with higher prediction error, with the most striking difference observed in Seaquest. The training scheme is identified as the major factor for improving long-term prediction, though the authors note it must be combined with an appropriate architecture to be effective. This interaction is a meaningful clarification, but it is not fully unpacked in the main text, and the architectural comparison deserved earlier placement in the paper rather than being deferred entirely to an appendix. The reviewer comment regarding schedule sampling is addressed through a comparison with Bengio et al., whose work used discrete data and shorter sequences—average sequence length of 11 in the Image Captioning example—where 100% Predicted Frames performed poorly. The authors argue their setting is substantively different. In simpler Atari games, the 100% Predicted Frames training scheme performs best, while in more complex games, schemes close to it are preferable. Oh et al. used a mixed training scheme without explanation, leaving the importance of various mixing strategies unclear in prior work. The authors' contribution here is therefore not simply a replication of prior findings. Section B.2 provides jumpy prediction analysis. The authors note that the Oh et al. model cannot be adapted for jumpy predictions because omitting intermediate frames removes action influence, which operates indirectly through frames. This is a technically precise and important distinction. The authors claim to be the first to demonstrate success with jumpy approaches for long-term prediction in large-scale domains—a notable claim, but one whose architectural reasoning is sound given the indirect action influence constraint. Breakout was excluded from the jumpy prediction analysis because its prediction error is uninformative, and the authors plan to add Riverraid experiments at subsequence length T of 15. The second reviewer comment—whether the current model's modification drives the jumpy prediction results or whether prior models like Oh et al. could achieve the same—is one the authors state they do not understand, and this impasse is itself informative. The jumpy simulator is more sensitive and fragile to structural changes than the single-step simulator, but achieves meaningful accuracy in a number of games, including Bowling, Freeway, Pong, and Fishing Derby, and can predict 100 time-steps into the future, distinguishing it from shorter-horizon prior work. The reviewer's concern remains only partially resolved, since the authors' explanation rests on the structural argument about indirect action influence rather than a direct empirical ablation against Oh et al. in the jumpy setting. Bengio et al.'s sequence length of 11 and discrete data setting do support the claim of a distinct contribution, but the authors should clarify in the main text—not only the appendix—why the Oh et al. architecture is structurally incompatible with jumpy prediction.

original: First, the bad: This paper is frustratingly written. The grammar is fine, but: - The first four pages are completely theoretical and difficult to follow without any concrete examples. These sections would benefit greatly from a common example woven through the different aspects of the theoretical discussion. - The ordering of the exposition is also frustrating. I found myself constantly having to refer ahead to figures and back to details that were important but seemingly presented out of order. Perhaps a reordering of some details could fix this. Recommendation: give the most naturally ordered oral presentation of the work and then order the paper similarly. Finally, the description of the experiments is cursory, and I found myself wondering whether the details omitted were important or not. Including experimental details in a supplementary section could help assuage these fears. The good: What the paper does well is to gather together past work on novelty generation and propose a unified framework in which to evaluate past and future models. This is done by repurposing existing generative model evaluation metrics for the task of evaluating novelty. The experiments are basic, but even the basic experiments go beyond previous work in this area (to this reviewer’s knowledge). Overall I recommend the paper be accepted, but I strongly recommend rewriting some components to make it more digestible. As with other novelty papers, it would be read thoroughly by the interested few, but it is likely to fight an uphill battle against the majority of readers outside the sub-sub-field of novelty generation; for this reason the theory should be made even more intuitive and clear and the experiments and results even more accessible.
sampled: This paper makes a solid contribution by using context-dependent word representations derived from hidden states of neural language models to improve sequence tagging in a semi-supervised setting. Evaluation on NER and chunking demonstrates state-of-the-art results on both tasks, and the included analysis addresses several natural questions about the method—showing in particular that language models trained on large data yield significant performance gains. This analysis is a genuine strength, giving readers a clearer picture of what drives the improvements. That said, several concerns should be addressed before publication. The most pressing methodological issue is that too many experiments appear to use the test set rather than held-out development data. Tables 5 and 6 should be revised to use development data to ensure a sound evaluation protocol and avoid comparisons that may be inflated by test set selection. The evaluation scope is also somewhat narrow. NER and chunking are standard benchmarks, but neither requires the model to capture interesting long-range dependencies, which limits what can be concluded about the representations more broadly. Experiments on tasks such as SRL or CCG supertagging would provide stronger evidence that the bidirectional language model representations generalize across a wider range of linguistic phenomena. Finally, the paper claims that a task-specific RNN is necessary because placing a CRF directly on top of the language model embeddings performs poorly, but it is not clear whether backpropagation into the language model was performed in that experiment. This detail matters for interpreting the result and should be clarified.
