sampled: The paper introduces LOTS, a method for layerwise origin-target synthesis, and the overall approach is sound. The core idea of using LOTS as a visualization technique for understanding intermediate feature layers in deep neural networks is genuinely original. The method goes beyond standard classification-based adversarial generation by matching features of an unrelated image—a meaningful extension—and it can generate adversarial examples for face-recognition models and other tasks outside classification. LOTS can also assess the invariance of learned features at any layer with respect to input class, and the methodology is applied to visualize the amount of perturbation needed to produce changes in higher-level features. The paper further proposes LOTS as a way to produce diverse adversarial examples for improving model robustness through training, which broadens its practical scope. That said, the analyses presented are relatively shallow and fail to address the most obvious questions a reader would raise about the method and its behavior. The visualizations are not particularly illuminating and make it difficult to draw meaningful conclusions, which weakens the paper's central contribution as a visualization and interpretability tool.

original: This paper investigates the application of distributional vectors of meaning in tasks that involve the identification of semantic relations, similar to the analogical reasoning task of Mikolov et al. (2013): Given an expression of the form “X is for France what London is for the UK”, X can be approximated by the simple vector arithmetic operation London-UK+France. The authors argue that this simple method can only capture very specific forms of analogies, and they present a measure that aims at identifying a wider range of relations in a more effective way. I admit I find the idea of a single vector space model being able to capture a number of semantic relationships and analogies rather radical and infeasible. As the authors mention in the paper, a number of studies already suggest for the opposite. The reason is quite simple: behind all these models lies (some form of) the distributional hypothesis (words in similar contexts have similar meanings), and this poses certain limitations in their expressive abilities; for example, words like “big” and “small” will always be considered as semantically similar from a vector perspective (although they express opposite meanings), since they occur in similar contexts. So I cannot see how the example given in Figure 1 is relevant to the very nature of vector spaces (or to any other semantic model for that matter!): there is a certain analogy between “man-king”, and “woman-queen”, but asking from a word space to capture “has-a” relationships of the form “owl-has-claws”, hence “hospital-has-walls”, doesn’t make much sense to me. The motivation behind the main proposal of the paper (a similarity measure that involves a form of cross-comparison between vectors of words and vectors representing the contexts of the words) is not clearly explained. Further, the measure is tested on the relation categories of the SemEval 2010 task with rather unsatisfactory results; in almost all cases, a simple baseline that takes into account only partial similarities between the tested word pairs present very high performance, with a difference from the best-performing model which seems to me statistically insignificant. So from both a methodological and an experimental perspective, the paper has weaknesses, and in its current form seems to describe work in progress; as such I am inclined against its presentation in ACL. (Formatting issue: The authors use the LaTeX styles for ACL 2016 — this should be fixed in case the paper is accepted). AUTHORS RESPONSE. Thank you for the clarifications.
sampled: The paper presents a genuinely novel reformulation of the GAN discriminator, replacing the traditional binary classifier with a component that assigns a scalar energy to each point in the generator's output domain. The optimality theorems concerning the Nash equilibrium are treated with sufficient rigor. One minor but meaningful imprecision appears in the abstract's use of "probabilistic GANs"; replacing this with "traditional" or "classical" GANs would better orient readers to what is being contrasted. The paper is well-written, and the hyperparameter exploration on MNIST is thorough. The semi-supervised results, showing that contrastive samples from the generator improve classification performance, represent a meaningful empirical contribution. That said, the relationship between this work and related efforts that broaden discriminator scope or use generative networks for contrastive samples in energy-based models—including arXiv 1511.06390 (Springenberg) and arXiv 1606.03439 (Kim and Bengio)—is not made sufficiently clear, and the manuscript should address this more directly. Theorem 2 also requires attention: the proof does not adequately establish why a Nash equilibrium exists for the proposed system. Separately, the phrase "Several papers were presented" in the prior work section should be replaced with more precise language. The discriminator is instantiated as an autoencoder, optionally paired with a PT regularizer that penalizes high cosine similarity among generated samples in a minibatch. However, the Inception score results are computed using vanilla EBGAN, making it difficult to isolate the PT regularizer's contribution to sample quality. Visual inspection alone is insufficient to conclude that EBGAN outperforms DC-GAN on LSUN and CelebA; a more systematic quantitative comparison is needed. The use of an Inception model trained on natural images to compute KL scores for MNIST is also questionable, and the authors should clarify whether this evaluation protocol is appropriate for that dataset. The model is novel and its core claims are supported by the optimality proofs and sample quality evidence across MNIST, LSUN, and CelebA. The concerns raised here—particularly around positioning relative to related work, the isolated assessment of the PT regularizer, and the quantitative comparison against DC-GAN—are real and should be addressed in revision.

original: The paper shows the relation between stochastically perturbing the parameter of a model at training time, and considering a mollified objective function for optimization. Aside from Eqs. 4-7 where I found hard to understand what the weak gradient g exactly represents, Eq. 8 is intuitive and the subsequent Section 2.3 clearly establishes for a given class of mollifiers the equivalence between minimizing the mollified loss and training under Gaussian parameter noise. The authors then introduce generalized mollifiers to achieve a more sophisticated annealing effect applicable to state-of-the-art neural network architectures (e.g. deep ReLU nets and LSTM recurrent networks). The resulting annealing effect can be counterintuitive: In Section 4, the Binomial (Bernoulli?) parameter grows from 0 (deterministic identity layers) to 1 (deterministic ReLU layers), meaning that the network goes initially through a phase of adding noise. This might effectively have the reverse effect of annealing. Annealing schemes used in practice seem very engineered (e.g. Algorithm 1 that determines how units are activated at a given layer consists of 9 successive steps). Due to the more conceptual nature of the authors contribution (various annealing schemes have been proposed, but the application of the mollifying framework is original), it could have been useful to reserve a portion of the paper to analyze simpler models with more basic (non-generalized) mollifiers. For example, I would have liked to see simple cases, where the perturbation schemes derived from the mollifier framework would be demonstrably more suitable for optimization than a standard heuristically defined perturbation scheme.
sampled: This paper makes three main contributions: a method for automatically generating large-scale pseudo training data for zero pronoun resolution, a two-step learning process that transfers knowledge from a large dataset to domain-specific data, and a tagging scheme that differentiates unknown words. The work is clearly written, and the experiments are well designed. The proposed approach achieves an absolute improvement of 3.1% F-score on OntoNotes 5.0 over state-of-the-art systems, which is a strong empirical result supporting the paper's central claims. Several clarifications are needed before the work can be fully evaluated. When the model predicts a pronoun but the head word of the candidate antecedent is not a pronoun, it is unclear how the system identifies the correct antecedent from prior context; this case should be addressed explicitly rather than left to the reader's inference. A related issue arises when the system predicts a noun that does not appear in the preceding content, since the mechanism for handling such cases is not described. It would also be useful to evaluate the system in two stages—first assessing the quality of model predictions and then measuring antecedent-finding performance separately—as this would clarify where errors originate. Finally, the choice of an attention-based neural network over alternative architectures is not justified, and a brief rationale for this design decision would strengthen the paper.

original: 1) Summary This paper proposes an end-to-end hybrid architecture to predict the local linear trends of time series. A temporal convnet on raw data extracts short-term features. In parallel, long term representations are learned via a LSTM on piecewise linear approximations of the time series. I think it is therefore not proper to call the proposed model a novel model with a new name Neural Graph Machine, but rather making it clear in the paper that this is an empirical study of the model proposed by Weston et al. 2012 to different problems would be more acceptable.

The Hessian weighting is well motivated and can be efficiently approximated via the Adam optimizer, removing the need to tune per-layer compression rates. The paper is easy to follow. While the uniform quantization plus Huffman coding contribution is not novel, its effectiveness is a useful finding. Hessian-weighted k-means stands out as a practical alternative to vanilla k-means solved by Lloyd’s algorithm, and the Adam-based approximation strengthens the method’s scalability. The explanation of storing additional bits for layer indication is unclear. The paper is a bit too long. The reviewer suggests clarifying the overhead of per-layer codebook storage, as the current description leaves ambiguity about how much extra cost this introduces in practice. The strong compression ratios for LeNet, the 32-layer ResNet, and AlexNet support the approach’s promise, but a clearer accounting of storage overhead would help readers assess the tradeoffs between the fixed-length Hessian-weighted scheme and variable-length uniform quantization with Huffman coding.

sampled: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: transfer in reinforcement learning across morphologically distinct agents. The core idea—using a shared skill to learn abstract feature spaces that then support transferring an unshared skill—is a promising hypothesis. The approach draws on methods that construct shared latent spaces, such as canonical correlation analysis, and the authors implement a three-layer neural network to learn these spaces. A simple CCA-based method is used as a baseline, but the evaluation would benefit from comparisons to more current techniques like manifold alignment or kernel CCA.

original: The paper discusses a method to learn interpretable hierarchical template representations from given data. The authors illustrate their approach on binary images. The paper presents a novel technique for extracting interpretable hierarchical template representations based on a small set of standard operations. It is then shown how a combination of those standard operations translates into a task equivalent to a boolean matrix factorization. This insight is then used to formulate a message passing technique which was shown to produce accurate results for these types of problems. Summary: ——— The paper presents an novel formulation for extracting hierarchical template representations that has not been discussed in that form. Unfortunately the experimental results are on smaller scale data and extension of the proposed algorithm to more natural images seems non-trivial to me. Quality: I think some of the techniques could be described more carefully to better convey the intuition. Clarity: Some of the derivations and intuitions could be explained in more detail. Originality: The suggested idea is reasonable but limited to binary data at this point in time. Significance: Since the experimental setup is somewhat limited according to my opinion, significance is hard to judge. Details: ——— 1. My main concern is related to the experimental evaluation.
sampled: This paper is clearly written and presents solid experimental results that offer new insights. The work merits publication and discussion given its significance. The paper empirically demonstrates that deep convolutional models require both depth and convolution: shallow student networks need multiple convolutional layers to match the accuracy of deep convolutional teachers on CIFAR-10. The experiments use L2 regression on logit outputs to train student networks, and the hyperparameter selection is thorough. These results partially contradict conclusions from Ba and Caruana 2014. That prior study suggested a different relationship between depth and model capacity, but the current findings challenge that view with careful evidence. The experimental design is rigorous, and the L2 regression on logits provides a clear framework for comparing student and teacher networks. The contradiction with Ba and Caruana 2014 is handled with appropriate nuance, and the paper does not overstate its claims. CIFAR-10 is a somewhat toy dataset with only 10 classes. The reviewer suggests testing on a more challenging problem such as ImageNet, which would strengthen the generalizability of the findings and address concerns about dataset simplicity. The paper merits publication. Its empirical contributions and the challenge to prior work make it a valuable addition to the literature on model distillation and network depth.

original: The paper claim that, when supported by a number of backup workers, synchronized-SGD actually works better than async-SGD. The paper first analyze the problem of staled updates in async-SGDs, and proposed the sync-SGD with backup workers. In the experiments, the authors shows the effectiveness of the proposed method in applications to Inception Net and PixelCNN. The idea is very simple, but in practice it can be quite useful in industry settings where adding some backup workders is not a big problem in cost. Nevertheless, I think the proposed solution is quite straightforward to come up with when we assume that each worker contains the full dataset and we have budge to add more workers. So, under this setting, it seems quite natural to have a better performance with the additional backup workers that avoid the staggering worker problem.
sampled: The paper presents a new dataset for evaluating outlier detection in word representations, covering five languages and constructed automatically from the Wikidata hierarchy. The reviewer recognizes that well-designed evaluation resources are valuable to the community. In the dataset, entities sharing a category form a cluster, and outliers are sampled at varying tree distances. A significant concern is the lack of discussion and comparison with existing approaches, especially since the proposed evaluation closely relates to entity typing, which the paper does not address. Heuristics are introduced to filter out uninteresting clusters, but the reviewer remains unconvinced that the dataset offers clear advantages over current resources. The reviewer also notes that LREC may be a more suitable venue than ICLR, given the resource-oriented nature of the work and the need for thorough comparison with prior methods.

original: This paper introduces CoopNets, an algorithm which trains a Deep-Energy Model (DEM, the “descriptor”) with the help of an auxiliary directed bayes net, e.g. “the generator”. The descriptor is trained via standard maximum likelihood, with Langevin MCMC for sampling. The generator is trained to generate likely samples under the DEM in a single, feed-forward ancestral sampling step. It can thus be used to shortcut expensive MCMC sampling, hence the reference to “cooperative training”. The above idea is interesting and novel, but unfortunately is not sufficiently validated by the experimental results. First and foremost, two out of the three experiments do not feature a train /test split, and ignore standard training and evaluation protocols for texture generation (see [R1]). Datasets are also much too small. As such these experiments only seem to confirm the ability of the model to overfit. On the third in-painting tasks, baselines are almost non-existent: no VAEs, RBMs, DEM, etc which makes it difficult to evaluate the benefits of the proposed approach. In a future revision, I would also encourage the authors to answer the following questions experimentally. What is the impact of the missing rejection step in Langevin MCMC (train with, without ?). What is the impact of the generator on the burn-in process of the Markov chain (show sample auto-correlation). How bad is approximation of training the generator from ({\tilde{Y}, \hat{X}) instead of ({\tilde{Y}, \tilde{X}) ? Run comparative experiments. The paper would also greatly benefit from a rewrite focusing on clarity, instead of hyperbole (“pioneering work” in reference to closely related, but non-peer reviewed work) and prose (“tale of two nets”). For example, the authors fail to specify the exact form of the energy function: this seems like a glaring omission. PROS: + Interesting and novel idea CONS: - Improper experimental protocols - Missing baselines - Missing diagnostic experiments [R1] Heess, N., Williams, C. K. I., and Hinton, G. E. (2009). Learning generative texture models with extended fields of-experts.
sampled: The idea of deriving actions from Class Activation Mapping visualizations is a creative adaptation of Zhou et al. 2016 to a reinforcement learning setting. Using tic-tac-toe as a toy problem to study CNN attention offers a controlled way to examine concept learning under weak supervision, and the CNN’s perfect accuracy on the labeling task provides a reliable basis for interpreting the visualizations. However, the paper does not compare to RL work that uses saliency maps to analyze network behavior, such as Simonyan et al. arXiv 2013, Wang et al. ICML 2016, and Zahavy et al. ICML 2016. It is unclear whether the distinction between “what will happen” and “what to do” is meaningful here, since the labels may coincide in many board states. This issue weakens the central claim that the CNN learns separate representations for prediction and decision. The dataset contains 1029 states with 18 classification labels covering two players and nine positions, but details about the test set composition and label distribution are missing. Without that information, it is hard to judge whether the perfect accuracy reflects genuine concept learning or label overlap. The claim that saliency maps cannot activate on constant-intensity grid squares is presented without supporting evidence or citation. The reviewer is also unsure how CAM is implemented without specifying a class of interest, since the original formulation requires a target class to generate the activation map. This technical ambiguity makes it difficult to evaluate the validity of the derived action policies. The experiments are novel but lack clear conclusions and broader context, leaving the contribution somewhat isolated from related work in deep reinforcement learning. The presentation would benefit from moving the Section 7 results alongside earlier discussions to improve narrative flow and reader comprehension. The meaning of “10^3 next to RCO” in Table 1 is unclear and should be clarified for reproducibility. Das et al.

original: The main concern raised in each review is the lack of a direct comparison of SSPNs to existing semantic segmentation benchmarks. We address this point here and then respond to each reviewer's other points directly. We’ve also made significant revisions to the structure and writing of the paper, particularly in the inference section, which we hope more clearly explains the intuitions behind InferSSPN. Despite not having comparisons on semantic segmentation benchmarks, SSPNs are a significant step forward in the state-of-the-art on scene understanding. SSPNs are (provably) more expressive than (and contain as a special case) MRFs and SPNs as commonly used for scene understanding and semantic segmentation, meaning that SSPNs are a richer model class than those already in use. Despite this increase in expressivity and complexity, InferSSPN is a very efficient (approximate) inference algorithm for the problem of parsing an image with respect to a grammar, which has been addressed by many previous works, but their approaches have all been very restrictive or inefficient. InferSSPN provably achieves low-order-polynomial time complexity for a problem with a state space that has size exponential in both the number of pixels and the height of the grammar. While the first version of the paper did not include accuracy results, as we thought the energy results were sufficient, we’ve since updated the paper to include all accuracy, energy, and time complexity results for all test cases. These show empirically that InferSSPN provides exponential improvements in time-complexity with no loss in accuracy relative to alpha-expansion, which provably returns local optima that are within a constant factor of the global optimum. Further, while we have characterized SSPNs in terms of scene understanding, they are as broadly applicable as SPNs and MRFs, and scene understanding is just the initial application we chose to focus on. Future applications may include activity recognition or social network modeling. Nonetheless, this paper presents a powerful new representation for efficiently modeling and reasoning about scenes at multiple levels of abstraction and is well within the scope of ICLR, which includes “hierarchical models” and “applications to vision” in its list of relevant topics. Learning SSPNs is important – both for evaluating SSPNs on existing semantic segmentation benchmarks and for their adoption in general – and is something that we are already working on. Unfortunately, there do not yet exist any image grammars or relevant datasets with which to train SSPNs, so learning requires either creating such datasets or learning with a large number of hidden variables. This is ongoing and future work.
sampled: The paper proposes using deep neural network features to construct a tree of life, which the reviewer finds creative but disconnected from biological practice. At its core, the approach reduces to hierarchical clustering of visual categories and offers little methodological novelty for the machine learning community. The reviewer doubts whether the resulting tree reveals anything meaningful about deep features or addresses a genuine need among biologists. The methodology lacks biological grounding in both construction and evaluation, relying on WordNet as an assumed ground-truth hierarchy without justifying why a lexical ontology should reflect evolutionary inheritance. By treating visual category relationships as strictly tree-like, the approach ignores the possibility that a graph structure would be more appropriate for capturing the complex associations present in visual data. The claim of human-competitive performance rests on qualitative comparisons rather than rigorous quantitative benchmarks, which substantially weakens the evidence. The reviewer questions whether recovering biological inheritance from purely visual inputs constitutes a meaningful scientific task, given that the visual world is not organized as a hierarchy even if the biological world can reasonably be defined as one. The absence of engagement with established phylogenetic methods or domain-specific evaluation protocols further undermines the work’s relevance to its stated audience. The overall impression is of a solution in search of a problem, with the application to biology serving more as a metaphorical framing than as a substantive contribution. The reviewer articulates this mismatch by observing that our visual world is not a hierarchy, while our biological world can reasonably be defined as one, highlighting the conceptual gap between the tree structure imposed on visual categories and the evolutionary relationships the paper claims to recover. This tension is never resolved through empirical validation or theoretical argument. Instead, the paper leans on the familiarity of ImageNet categories and WordNet structure without interrogating whether these resources are fit for the biological task at hand. Reliance on deep neural networks as feature extractors does not compensate for the weak evaluation design, since the features themselves are never analyzed in terms of what they encode about biological similarity. The qualitative results do not persuade the reviewer that the recovered tree captures inheritance rather than superficial visual resemblance, and the absence of quantitative metrics makes it impossible to assess the claimed human-competitive performance. The work would benefit from a clearer problem definition grounded in actual biological questions and from evaluation protocols that measure success against established phylogenetic baselines. Without such grounding, the paper remains an intriguing but unconvincing exploration that does not advance understanding of deep features or biological classification. The reviewer sees limited value in its current form for either the computer vision or the computational biology community.

original: This paper proposed a very interesting idea of using cognitive features for sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection. The authors claim that this is the first work to include cognitive features into the NLP community. Strength: 1. The paper is generally well written and easy to follow 2. Very interesting idea which may inspire research in other NLP tasks. Weakness: 1. The motivation of using cognitive features for sentiment analysis is not very well justified. I can imagine these features may help reflect the reading ease, but I don't see why they are helpful in detecting sentiment polarities. 2. sampled: The paper proposes an extension of PixelCNN conditioned on text and spatially-structured constraints, similar to Reed 2016a but built on PixelCNN rather than a GAN. The authors do not claim that the conditional PixelCNN outperforms a conditional GAN, and the technical novelty is incremental. The paper would benefit from a discussion of the trade-offs between PixelCNN and GAN-based approaches, as well as an analysis of training and generation time. No quantitative comparisons are included, and given that, more than three visual examples would be appropriate. The generated results look reasonably good and show sufficient diversity, though color mistakes remain an issue. original: This paper develops Submodular Sum Product Networks (SSPNs) and an efficient inference algorithm for approximately computing the most probable labeling of variables in the model. The main application in the paper is on scene parsing. In this context, SSPNs define an energy function with a grammar component for representing a hierarchy of labels and an MRF for encoding smoothness of labels over space. To perform inference, the authors develop a move-making algorithm, somewhat in the spirit of fusion moves (Lempitsky et al., 2010) that repeatedly improves a solution by considering a large neighborhood of alternative segmentations and solving an optimization problem to choose the best neighbor. Empirical results show that the proposed algorithm achieves better energy that belief propagation of alpha expansion and is much faster. This is generally a well-executed paper. The model is interesting and clearly defined, the algorithm is well presented with proper analysis of the relevant runtimes and guarantees on the behavior. Overall, the algorithm seems effective at minimizing the energy of SSPN models. Having said that, I don't think this paper is a great fit for ICLR. The model is even somewhat to the antithesis of the idea of learning representations, in that a highly structured form of energy function is asserted by the human modeller, and then inference is performed. I don't see the connection to learning representations. One additional issue is that while the proposed algorithm is faster than alternatives, the times are still on the order of 1-287 seconds per image, which means that the applicability of this method (as is) to something like training ConvNets is limited. Finally, there is no attempt to argue that the model produces better segmentations than alternative models. The only evaluations in the paper are on energy values achieved and on training data.
sampled: The paper builds directly on the framework introduced by Weston (2016) and applies end-to-end memory networks to a dialogue setting where a teacher provides feedback. The dialogue itself is quite constrained and functions more like a question answering task than a genuine conversational exchange. The main contribution lies in demonstrating that the model also works when data is collected online—that is, using the agent’s own policy rather than a fixed policy defined beforehand. This shift to an online data collection paradigm via Mechanical Turk is a meaningful practical step. It requires only modest algorithmic changes, primarily the introduction of epsilon-greedy exploration, which limits the model novelty. The writing is clear and the paper tests several interesting models. The experimental design is easy to follow and the comparisons are laid out straightforwardly. The reliance on Mechanical Turk for human feedback is appropriate for the scale of the study. The central point the authors stress is that the model also works with online data collection, and this fairly captures where the novelty actually resides. I see value in showing that the approach can function outside a static offline dataset. However, adding human testing data alone is not sufficient for a conference paper at a venue like ICLR, and the core architecture remains largely unchanged from prior work. The paper is borderline. The online collection setup is a genuine contribution, but the dialogue setting is too narrow to fully convince as a dialogue learning advance. I updated the score after the author response emphasized real-world implementation as a contribution, which helped clarify the practical motivation.

original: This work proved to be a controversial submission. This paper has two main components: 1) a neural framework TBRU/DRAGNN, 2) experimental results on some NLP tasks. Generally there was lack of consensus about the originality of (1) and a general feeling that even if there are aspect of novelties, that the paper was lacking clarity about is contributions One reviewer was an outlier, highlighting the benefit of the ability "incorporate dynamic recurrent connections through the definition of the transition system" which is claimed to be really novel. sampled: This paper presents an interesting idea connected to John McCarthy's foundational work on learning from advice, implemented here using a deep learning controller. While the direction is promising, the description of the proposed architecture is confusing, making it difficult to assess the technical novelty of the controller. The experiments are conducted in a simplistic 2D maze environment, which is not sufficient to demonstrate the system's capabilities. A more convincing evaluation would test the approach on more complex and varied tasks, such as Atari games or physics simulators. The current results do not provide enough evidence that the system can handle advice more complex than that shown in the simple maze. For instance, the system should be able to interpret high-level instructions in a more dynamic environment, analogous to telling a human to "keep a certain distance from the car in front."

original: This paper proposes to learn groups of orthogonal features in a convnet by penalizing correlation among features in each group. The technique is applied in the setting of image classification with “privileged information” in the form of foreground segmentation masks, where the model is trained to learn orthogonal groups of foreground and background features using the correlation penalty and an additional “background suppression” term. Pros: Proposes a “group-wise model diversity” loss term which is novel, to my knowledge. The use of foreground segmentation masks to improve image classification is also novel. The method is evaluated on two standard and relatively large-scale vision datasets: ImageNet and PASCAL VOC 2012. Cons: The evaluation is lacking. There should be a baseline that leaves out the background suppression term, so readers know how much that term is contributing to the performance vs. the group orthogonal term. The use of the background suppression term is also confusing to me -- it seems redundant, as the group orthogonality term should already serve to suppress the use of background features by the foreground feature extractor. It would be nice to see the results with “Incomplete Privileged Information” on the full ImageNet dataset (rather than just 10% of it) with the privileged information included for the 10% of images where it’s available. This would verify that the method and use of segmentation masks remains useful even in the regime of more labeled classification data. The presentation overall is a bit confusing and difficult to follow, for me. For example, Section 4.2 is titled “A Unified Architecture: GoCNN”, yet it is not an overview of the method as a whole, but a list of specific implementation details (even the very first sentence). Minor: calling eq 3 a “regression loss” and writing “||0 - x||” rather than just “||x||” is not necessary and makes understanding more difficult -- I’ve never seen a norm regularization term written this way or described as a “regression to 0”. Minor: in fig. 1 I think the FG and BG suppression labels are swapped: e.g., the “suppress foreground” mask has 1s in the FG and 0s in the BG (which would suppress the BG, not the FG). An additional question: why are the results in Table 4 with 100% privileged information different from those in Table 1-2? Are these not the same setting? The ideas presented in this paper are novel and show some promise, but are currently not sufficiently ablated for readers to understand what aspects of the method are important.
sampled: This paper introduces NewsQA, a machine comprehension dataset of over 100,000 question-answer pairs from 10,000 CNN news articles. However, the work appears to have been prepared in a hurry, which raises concerns about the quality of the dataset and the soundness of the analysis. The primary issue is the potential for noise introduced during data collection. I question the decision not to show the news article to crowdworkers as they created questions. Human performance on NewsQA is reported at 74.9%, which seems low for this type of task. The paper suggests the SQuAD dataset may not be hard enough, based on the rapid improvement in machine performance on that benchmark. Machine performance on SQuAD was 51% at submission, but the leaderboard's best performance had reached 82% by the time of this paper's writing. A significant discrepancy exists regarding human performance on SQuAD, which undermines confidence in the current paper's evaluation. The authors measure human performance on SQuAD between 70.5% and 82%, while the original SQuAD paper reported a range of 80.3% to 90.5%. The reported 74.9% human performance on NewsQA is concerning. This low figure might indicate noise from the data collection methodology rather than the true difficulty of the questions. The performance gap between humans and machines on NewsQA is stated to be 25.3% F1, but this gap is less meaningful if the human baseline itself is compromised by noise. To avoid collecting trivial questions, a better design could have required crowdworkers to create questions that an existing, state-of-the-art QA system cannot answer correctly. The NewsQA dataset is built upon a larger subset of the CNN/Daily Mail corpus than SQuAD, using 12,000 articles compared to SQuAD's 500. The paper was submitted to EMNLP’16, and the dataset is constructed from CNN news articles from the CNN/Daily Mail corpus. The work seems rushed, raising doubts about the dataset's quality. The low human performance on NewsQA (74.9%) is a major point of concern, as it might reflect noise from the data collection process rather than inherent task difficulty, especially given the discrepancy between the authors' measurement of human performance on SQuAD (70.5-82%) and what was originally reported (80.3-90.5%).

original: This work proposes a method for segmenting target generation sequence that is learned as part of the model. Generally all reviewers found this paper novel and interesting. Pros: - Quality: The paper is both containing "with solid theoretically justified" and "present(s) nice improvements over character based result". sampled: This paper presents a recurrent neural network for stochastic volatility modeling of financial time series. The model parameters are learned by maximizing the marginal likelihood via a variational approximation. The authors report that their model outperforms parametric GARCH models and a Gaussian process volatility model on both synthetic and real-world data. An RNN-based inference network is used to approximate the posterior distribution of the latent variables. The proposed method seems technically sound, with one exception in the description of the inference model. There appears to be an error in equation (19). The inference model as described is performing filtering, not smoothing, as the posterior distribution for a given time step depends only on past and current observations.

original: In this interesting paper the authors explore the idea of using an ensemble of multiple discriminators in generative adversarial network training. This comes with a number of benefits, mainly being able to use less powerful discriminators which may provide better training signal to the generator early on in training when strong discriminators might overpower the generator. My main comment is about the way the paper is presented. The caption of Figure 1. and Section 3.1 suggests using the best discriminator by taking the maximum over the performance of individual ensemble members. This does not appear to be the best thing to do because we are just bound to get a training signal that is stricter than any of the individual members of the ensemble.
sampled: This paper proposes a simple method for augmenting neural language models with an external cache that acts as a copying mechanism for recent words. The mechanism is efficient, scales to large cache sizes, and improves language modeling performance on RNN baselines without requiring long-term backpropagation. The experiments are convincing. A key insight is that using past hidden states as keys and the current hidden state as a query is effective without backpropagation tuning. The simplicity and efficiency of this approach are its main strengths. My primary criticism is the work's incremental nature, which might make it a better fit for a more specialized NLP venue. However, the simple yet effective approach is valuable to the community and warrants publication.

original: This paper presents three improvements to the standard LSTM architecture used in many neural NLP models: Monte Carlo averaging, embed average pooling, and residual connections. Each of the modifications is trivial to implement, so the paper is definitely of interest to any NLP researchers experimenting with deep learning. With that said, I am concerned about the experiments and their results. The residual connections do not seem to consistently help performance; on SST the vertical residuals help but the lateral residuals hurt, and on IMDB it is the opposite. More fundamentally, there need to be more tasks than just sentiment analysis here. I'm not quite sure why the paper's focus is on text classification, as any NLP task using an LSTM encoder could conceivably benefit from these modifications. It would be great to see a huge variety of tasks like QA, MT, etc., which would really make the paper much stronger.
sampled: This paper proposes a generalization of layered neural architectures, the "Multiagent System for Layer Free Network," where nodes communicate via messages. However, the presentation is unclear, making it difficult to assess the work's contribution. The low-level details of the proposed method are particularly confusing. A central argument seems circular: the paper demonstrates that the layer-free architecture can perform the same computation as a standard MLP, which calls into question the novelty and practical benefit of the approach. For instance, while the work aims to move beyond matrix-vector products, Algorithm 4 uses them for both the forward and backward passes. The "locking" nature of the computation also suggests that an asynchronous implementation would be equivalent to a standard one, undermining a key motivation for the new architecture.

original: This paper presents an multi-view learning algorithm which projects the inputs of different views (linearly) such that the neighborhood relationship (transition probabilities) agree across views. This paper has good motivation--to study multi-view learning from a more information retrieval perspective. Some concerns: -- The time complexity of the algorithm in its current form is high (see last paragraph of page 4). This might be the reason why the authors have conducted experiments on small datasets, and using linear projections. -- The proposed method does have some nice properties, e.g., it does not require the projections to have the same dimension across views (I like this). While it more directly models neighborhood relationship than CCA based approaches, it is still not directly optimizing typical retrieval (e.g., ranking-based) criteria. On the other hand, the contrastive loss in Hermann and Blunsom. Multilingual Distributed Representations without Word Alignment. ICLR 2014. is certainly a relevant "information retrieval" approach, and shall be discussed and compared with. My major concern about this paper is the experiments. As I mentioned in my previous comments, there are limited cases where linear mapping is more desirable than nonlinear mappings for dimension reduction. While the authors have argued that linear projection may provide better interpretability, I have not found empirical justification in this paper. Moreover, one could achieve interpretability by visualizing the projections and see what variations of the input is reflected along certain dimensions; this is commonly done for nonlinear dimension reduction methods.
sampled: This paper proposes an unsupervised, encoder-decoder model for learning generic feature representations from graph structures. The model is trained to predict random walk sequences, adapting an approach from natural language processing to map structurally similar subgraphs to nearby points in the embedding space. While the model is reported to achieve good results on several real-world classification tasks, the evaluation has some weaknesses. The paper lacks clarity on certain constraints, such as the relationship "l_min >= (n_k - 1), … >= l_max". The primary concern is the comparison to existing methods, many of which use task-specific supervised techniques. As another reviewer noted, the same classifier should be used for all compared methods to ensure a fair evaluation. The presentation of results in Sections 3 and 4 needs clarification. For example, the comparison to Deep Graph Kernels in Section 3.2 is not well-justified, and the discussion comparing the method with LINE and ECFP in Section 3.3 is underdeveloped. A more direct comparison under equivalent conditions would be necessary to substantiate the claims of achieving state-of-the-art results. The authors state their goal is to develop a generic, unsupervised feature representation, which is a valuable contrast to supervised approaches requiring feature engineering, but the current evaluation does not fully support the claimed advantages.

original: The authors provide an approach to policy learning skills via a stochastic neural network representation. The overall idea seems novel, and the reviewers are in agreement that the method provides an interesting take on skill learning. The additional visualization presented in response to the reviewer comments were also quite useful. Pros: + Conceptually nice approach to skill learning in RL + Strong results on benchmark tasks Cons: - The overall clarity of the paper could still be improved: the actual algorithmic section seems to present the methods still at a very high level, though code release may also help with this (it would not be at all trivial to re-implement the method just given the paper).
sampled: This paper presents a small but effective extension to the Neural Programmer-Interpreter that enables recursion, allowing the model to generalize better from fewer execution traces. The work is a good example of how a modest addition can improve the practicality of a machine learning method. original: We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments and suggestions. We’ve uploaded a revision with an expanded introduction which clarifies the motivation for BiGAN and the theory in Section 3 in the context of feature learning. Note that our theoretical arguments go beyond simply showing that BiGAN maintains the properties of the original GAN framework. In particular, we show that the BiGAN objective is equivalent to that of an “L0 autoencoder”, encouraging the encoder and generator to invert one another (Theorem 3). If fully optimized, the encoder and generator are inverses of one another almost everywhere (Theorem 2). The algorithm offers an efficient solution with minimal additional computational or memory demands relative to traditional beam search techniques, making it an appealing choice for diverse decoding tasks. In applications like image captioning, machine translation, conversation generation, and visual question answering, DBS demonstrates its versatility and effectiveness in producing diverse and accurate outputs. Overall, DBS surpasses conventional beam search approaches and other diverse decoding methods, establishing itself as a valuable tool for improving output diversity and quality across various tasks.

The question of the (arguably mild) inconsistency of applying a linear dimensionality reduction algorithm, that is trained without any sigmoid, and then passing its learned representation through a sigmoid is not even raised. This, in addition to the fact that sigmoid hidden layers are no longer commonly used (why did you not also consider using RELUs?). More importantly I suspect methodological problems with the experimental comparisons: the paper mentions using *default* values for learning-rate and momentum, and having (arbitrarily?) fixed epoch to 400 (no early stopping?) and L2 regularization to 1e-4 for some models. *All* hyper parameters should always be properly hyper-optimized using a validation set (or cross-validation) including early-stopping, and this separately for each model under comparison (ideally also including layer sizes). This is all the more important since you are considering smallish datasets, so that the various initialization strategies act mainly as different indirect regularization schemes: they thus need to be carefully tuned. The reviewer suggested that the experiments could be improved to make the results more convincing and practically useful, with the validity of the experiments potentially enhanced by providing more evidence and thorough analysis. In conclusion, "Modularized Morphing of Neural Networks" offers a novel approach to network morphism. Despite its initial non-acceptance at the ICML 2016 conference, the research and proposed method hold significant potential. The authors' exploration of morphing a convolutional layer into an arbitrary module of a neural network is a substantial contribution to the field. The reviewer's suggestion to improve the experiments provides a valuable avenue for the authors to make their results more convincing and practically useful in the future. The paper's importance and potential impact should not be overlooked despite its initial non-acceptance.

sampled: The paper "Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks for Resource Efficient Inference" presents a new approach to pruning convolutional kernels in neural networks. This method uniquely applies a criterion based on the mathematical principle of Taylor expansion. It demonstrates superior performance compared to other pruning criteria for large Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The method is also applicable to transfer learning, where large pretrained networks are tailored for specific tasks. One of the paper's key strengths is the theoretical reduction it can achieve. In particular, pruning can lead to more than a 10x decrease in the size of adapted 3D-convolutional filters. This significant reduction highlights the proposed method's potential to enhance the efficiency of resource-demanding inference tasks. The method's effectiveness is further confirmed through testing on the extensive ImageNet dataset. Its successful application to fine-grained classification tasks, as demonstrated by its performance on the Birds-200 and Flowers-102 datasets, further validates the paper's contributions.

original: We thank the reviewers for several helpful suggestions. We first address the issues raised by two or more reviewers here. As a general comment, we would like to emphasize again the exploratory nature of our work. We aimed to explore the following question: is it possible for a recurrent model to (cheaply) determine a priori how much computation it is going to need at each time step? We designed our model and experimental section with this interrogation in mind, and believe that we were able to provide a positive answer. As regards the wall-clock time, the computational gains are currently, to quote Reviewer 2 conceptual only, as we are using the Torch GPU kernels, and optimizing the hardware implementation was beyond the scope of this project. Our goal was to make the possible implications of the result clear, but we will clarify the language of the paper to reflect this more accurately. For each experiment, we tried a range of \bar{m} values for the Variable Computation recurrent network and a range of hidden state dimensions for its vanilla counterpart. While we only provided one result on PTB, Figure 5 illustrates how both of these choices affect the model’s computation and perplexity on a Czech and a German dataset; note that the Variable Computation curve for perplexity/number of operations is always under the Vanilla one, meaning fewer operations for a better perplexity. We will provide the same figure for PTB. Our original reasoning for only providing vanilla RNN results on PTB was that we were trying to compare apples to apples, so to speak, and to reinforce the message that we are considering a paradigm which can be extended to other architectures. However, we have since successfully applied our method to the GRU architecture, which gives us the Variable Computation Gated Recurrent Unit (VCGRU).
sampled: The paper "Deep Character-Level Neural Machine Translation By Learning Morphology" introduces an innovative adaptation of encoder-decoder neural MT, marking a considerable advancement in the field of neural machine translation and morphology learning. The authors' decision to release their code and final learned models is commendable and beneficial to the research community. However, there appears to be an inconsistency in the paper's depiction of its system. The text refers to a 6-level architecture, but the diagram shows fewer than 6 layers. This discrepancy could potentially confuse readers and future researchers attempting to replicate the study. Additionally, the paper does not explicitly state which WMT test and development sets underpin the reported results. This lack of clarity complicates comparisons with other systems in the field. The results also do not align with the state-of-the-art results for other types of MT system, suggesting room for improvement. A more comprehensive background context could have enriched the paper. For example, the authors could have offered more information on the specific tasks of En-Fr and En-Cs translation, and how their proposed model enhances performance and efficiency in these tasks. Moreover, the instructions in the software README could be more detailed. While the authors' decision to make their code and models available is laudable, incomplete or unclear instructions could hinder others from using or building upon their work. This is particularly important given the unique approach to character-level translation using an encoder-decoder architecture. The system's performance after just one training epoch is impressive, achieving a higher BLEU score than the bpe-based model. This suggests the system's efficiency and its ability to learn effective morphological tokenizations. However, it's worth noting that these results are based on the newstest2015 dataset for testing and the newstest2013 dataset for development.

original: Hi, I'm one of the authors of Bowman et al. 2016, and I wanted to point out that while our description of the difficulties in training RNN type models with global latent variables occurs in a section called "Optimization Challenges," we make similar observations as you do in your paper, namely that having a very powerful decoder model like an RNN can result in the model ignoring the global latent variable even at the optimum (perhaps the section should have more generally been called "Learning Challenges"). Specifically, we found that without using "word dropout" in the decoder, which effectively weakens the decoder model and forces the global variable to encode more information, we would not learn a useful latent variable. In our Figure 3, we show the results of using different amounts of word dropout and how the proportional split between the global latent code KL and the p(x|z) likelihood changes, even though the total lower bound always gets worse.
sampled: The paper titled "A Transition-Based Directed Acyclic Graph Parser for UCCA" introduces UCCA as a target representation for semantic parsing, a significant development in the field of semantic representation. The authors also present a transition-based parser for inference into UCCA, which, while derived from existing transition-based schemes, includes valuable extensions that make it applicable in this domain. This adaptation highlights the paper's strength in dealing with complex concepts such as DAG structures, discontinuous structures, and non-terminal nodes. The empirical evaluation of the parser also shows promising results when compared to several credible baselines. However, the paper lacks a multilingual evaluation, a crucial aspect considering the global application of semantic parsers. The authors' use of the term 'grammarless' to describe their model is also somewhat unclear and could benefit from further explanation. Despite these areas for improvement, the paper provides a robust exploration of a transition-based parser using UCCA and bidirectional LSTMs.

original: This paper introduces a hierarchical clustering method using learned CNN features to build 'the tree of life'. The assumption is that the feature similarity indicates the distance in the tree. The authors tried three different ways to construct the tree: 1) approximation central point 2) minimum spanning tree and 3) multidimensional scaling based method. Out of them, MDS works the best. It is a nice application of using deep features. However, I lean toward rejecting the paper because the following reasons: 1) All experiments are conducted in very small scale. The experiments include 6 fish species, 11 canine species, 8 vehicle classes. There are no quantitative results, only by visualizing the generated tree versus the wordNet tree. Moreover, the assumption of using wordNet is not quite valid. WordNet is not designed for biology purpose and it might not reflect the true evolutionary relationship between species. 2) Limited technical novelty. Most parts of the pipeline are standard, e.g. use pretrained model for feature extraction, use previous methods to construct hierarchical clustering. I think the technical contribution of this paper is very limited.
sampled: The paper, "Learning through Dialogue Interactions by Asking Questions," delves into the potential of dialogue agents to learn through question-asking interactions. The concept is compelling and the study's design, which incorporates a simulator and synthetic tasks within the movie domain, is noteworthy. The range of environment-scenario combinations tested provides a broad spectrum of experimental designs. However, some tasks may be overly simplistic, possibly diminishing the complexity and depth of the learning process. This brings me to the observation that the synthetic environment used seems somewhat constrained, lacking the depth typically found in human-chatbot interactions. I do acknowledge that the 'ground-up' approach, which begins with simple environments, is indeed a valuable area of exploration. In the second half of my review, I want to point out that the simulation of the initial error a learner could make during dialogue is somewhat limited. This could restrict the comprehensive testing of the dialogue agents' learning abilities. Additionally, the paper could strengthen its validity by incorporating human experiments.

original: This paper gives a theoretical motivation for tieing the word embedding and output projection matrices in RNN LMs. The argument uses an augmented loss function which spreads the output probability mass among words with close word-embedding. I see two main drawbacks from this framework: The augmented loss function has no trainable parameters and is used for only for regularization. This is not expected to give gains with large enough datasets. The augmented loss is heavily “engineered” to produce the desired result of parameter tying. It’s not clear what happens if you try to relax it a bit, by adding parameters, or estimating y~ in a different way. Nevertheless the argument is very interesting, and clearly written. The simulated results indeed validate the argument, and the PTB results seem promising. Minor comments: Section 3: Can you clarify if y~ is conditioned on the t example or on the entire history. Eq. 3.
sampled: The study, "Adjusting for Dropout Variance in Batch Normalization and Weight Initialization," presents an innovative weight initialization technique to mitigate the variance caused by dropout. This unique approach contributes fresh insights to the ongoing dialogue about dropout variance and its impact on neural networks. Moreover, the authors suggest modifications to Batch Normalization to accommodate the dropout variance, a significant move that paves the way for incorporating dropout variance adjustments into prevailing normalization methods. The proposed techniques were evaluated using the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, both of which are well-regarded and frequently employed in related studies. The findings showed improved accuracy over conventional methods, such as Monte Carlo dropout, underscoring the effectiveness of the new method. The potential impact of this study is substantial, given its relevance to a variety of models regularly used in the field.

original: Strengths: This paper presents an approach to creating concept maps using crowdsourcing. The general ideas are interesting and the main contribution lies in the collection of the dataset. As such, I imagine that the dataset will be a valuable resource for further research in this field. Clearly a lot of effort has gone into this work. Weaknesses: Overall I felt this paper a bit overstated in placed. As an example, the authors claim a new crowdsourcing scheme as one of their contributions. This claims is quite strong though and it reads more like the authors are applying best practice in crowdsourcing to their work. This isn’t a novel methods then, it’s rather a well thought and sound application of existing knowledge. Similarly, the authors claim that they develop and present a new corpus. This seems true and I can see how a lot of effort was invested in its preparation, but then Section 4.1 reveals that actually this is based on an existing dataset. Where do the clusters come from? Are they part of the TAC2008b dataset? In 4.6 expert annotators are used to create the gold standard concept maps. sampled: The data appear to be well collected, and the empirical presentation is a clear strength. My main concern is that many of the conclusions are not especially unexpected given the measurements described. The paper would be stronger if it more clearly separated the value of the data collection from claims that may already follow from standard expectations about DNNs on GPU hardware. This distinction is important for assessing novelty. Finding #1 presents power consumption as independent of batch size and architecture, while I read the evidence as indicating similarly high GPU use across architectures and batch sizes. That interpretation is plausible, but it also makes the finding less surprising. If the GPU is effectively fully used in each tested condition, then stable power behavior across DNN architectures and batch sizes would be expected. The more notable result may therefore be the equal apparent use of GPU compute resources across the tested models, rather than the broader formulation of the finding. Figure 9 is central to the argument about accuracy and inference time. I agree that a linear pattern in Figure 9 could imply the stated hyperbolic relation. The difficulty is that Finding #2 does not seem well supported for newer model generations, since newer models cluster in the upper-left area of Figure 9. That clustering weakens the claim that the relationship is asymptotically hyperbolic, and the paper should be more cautious about extending the pattern beyond the displayed evidence.

original: This paper considers the problem of KB completion and proposes ITransF for this purpose. Unlike STransE that assigns each relation an independent matrix, this paper proposes to share the parameters between different relations. A model is proposed where a tensor D is constructed that contains various relational matrices as its slices and a selectional vector \alpha is used to select a subset of relevant relational matrix for composing a particular semantic relation. The paper then discuss a technique to make \alpha sparse. Experimental results on two standard benchmark datasets shows the superiority of ITransF over prior proposals. The paper is overall well written and the experimental results are good. However, I have several concerns regarding this work that I hope the authors will answer in their response. 1. Just by arranging relational matrices in a tensor and selecting (or more appropriately considering a linearly weighted sum of the relational matrices) does not ensure any information sharing between different relational matrices. This would have been the case if you had performed some of a tensor decomposition and projected the different slices (relational matrices) into some common lower-dimensional core tensor. It is not clear why this approach was not taken despite the motivation to share information between different relational matrices. 2. The two requirements (a) to share information across different relational matrices and (b) make the attention vectors sparse are some what contradictory. If the attention vector is truly sparse and has many zeros then information will not flow into those slices during optimisation. 3. The authors spend a lot of space discussing techniques for computing sparse attention vectors. The authors mention in page 3 that \ell_1 regularisation did not work in their preliminary experiments. However, no experimental results are shown for \ell_1 regularisation nor they explain why \ell_1 is not suitable for this task. To this reviewer, it appears as an obvious baseline to try, especially given the ease of optimisation. You use \ell_0 instead and get into NP hard optimisations because of it. Then you propose a technique and a rather crude approximation in the end to solve it. All that trouble could be spared if \ell_1 was used. 4. The vector \alpha is performing a selection or a weighing over the slices of D. It is slightly misleading to call this as “attention” as it is a term used in NLP for a more different type of models (see attention model used in machine translation). 5. It is not clear why you need to initialise the optimisation by pre-trained embeddings from TransE. Why cannot you simply randomly initialise the embeddings as done in TransE and then update them? It is not fair to compare against TransE if you use TransE as your initial point. Learning the association between semantic relations is an idea that has been used in related problems in NLP such as relational similarity measurement [Turney JAIR 2012] and relation adaptation [Bollegala et al. IJCAI 2011]. It would be good to put the current work with respect to such prior proposals in NLP for modelling inter-relational correlation/similarity. Thanks for providing feedback. I have read it.
sampled: The paper, Cortical-Inspired Open-Bigram Representation for Handwritten Word Recognition, studies distant bigram representations inspired by cortical evidence for handwritten word recognition. The submission is generally well written, and its focus on open-bigrams creates a clear link between cognitive reading research and recognition modeling. The experiments on Rimes and IAM are appropriate for the stated task, and using LSTM-RNNs trained to predict open-bigrams gives a concrete framework for comparing representations. My main concern is the comparison between the proposed method and the standard baseline. The paper should give more detail on this comparison, since the current presentation does not make the basis for the claimed advantage sufficiently clear. The evaluation would be stronger with model complexity information for all systems being compared. In particular, parameter counts are needed to judge whether the observed differences come from the representation itself or from differences in capacity. The paper should also include language models in the evaluation. Different context levels may change the impact of language models, which is important for assessing the relative value of the proposed representation. The claim in section 5 that the approach obtains competitive or better error rates would be easier to evaluate if these comparisons were included. The restricted comparative corpus is another important issue. Only longer words are used in the comparative experiments. This leaves 70% of the data, and the paper should quantify the effect of using this restricted corpus. Without that evidence, it is hard to know whether the reported comparison reflects the method or the selected subset. The decision to ignore order also needs stronger justification. Handwritten word recognition is a monotonic sequential classification task, so it is not obvious that ignoring order is decision-theoretically justified. An experiment that varies only the use of order would help isolate the effect of this design choice. Such an experiment could separate the contribution of open-bigram content from the contribution of ordering information. The paper should also clarify several local points. At the end of page 1, please explain the phrase "whole language method". On page 6, please define the notation rnn_d(x,t). The discussion of order should distinguish order 0, order 1, and higher orders more carefully. In Table 2, precision and recall are not directly comparable between order 0 and higher orders because the target counts differ, which affects how the table should be interpreted. The text should state this limitation explicitly. The comparison between order 0 and larger orders should avoid implying that the same target population is being measured. This clarification is especially important because order 0 corresponds effectively to unigrams. The higher-order results therefore combine differences in representation with differences in target counts. The manuscript would benefit from making that distinction clearer in the table discussion. These issues do not undermine the topic, but they do limit the strength of the experimental claims. The paper presents a promising idea, but the evidence should more directly support the proposed comparison.

original: Interesting paper which proposes jointly learning automatic segmentation of words to sub words and their acoustic models. Although the training handles the word segmentation as hidden variable which depends also on the acoustic representations, during the decoding only maximum approximation is used. The authors present nice improvements over character based results, however they did not compare results with word segmentation which does not assume the dependency on acoustic. Obviously, only text based segmentation would result in two (but simpler) independent tasks. In order to extract such segmentation several publicly open tools are available and should be cited. Some of those tools can also exploit the unigram probabilities of the words to perform their segmentations. It looks that the improvements come from the longer acoustical units - longer acoustical constraints which could lead to less confused search -, pointing towards full word models. In another way, less tokens are more probable due to less multiplication of probabilities. As a thought experiment for an extreme case: if all the possible segmentations would be possible (mixture of all word fragments, characters, and full-words), would the proposed model use word fragments at all? (WSJ is a closed vocabulary task). It would be good to show that the sub word model could outperform even a full-word model (no segmentation).
sampled: The idea in Lossy Image Compression with Compressive Autoencoders is interesting and well motivated, particularly as a neural autoencoder approach to lossy image compression. The main empirical concern is that the method achieves rates essentially comparable to JPEG 2000, which weakens the case for a deep autoencoder compression scheme in its current form. Automatically learned compression schemes could be useful in settings where expert knowledge is limited, so the submission addresses a worthwhile direction, but the potential is not yet supported by sufficient analysis or comparative evidence. The paper is not suitable for publication in its current version. A key missing analysis is how the learned encoder relates to JPEG 2000. The authors should examine whether the learned filters resemble those used in JPEG 2000 or are substantially different. The evaluation should also provide texture-specific evidence showing where the method improves and where it fails, rather than relying only on aggregate performance against the baseline. Showing the 10 best and worst image patches across bit-rates would make the strengths and failure modes more concrete. The paper also needs to establish that any gains come from the coding scheme itself, rather than only from a stronger decoder, for example by testing a decoder trained using JPEG 2000 codes and possibly encoded random projections.

original: The authors explore the idea of deep-learning a static analyzer. They do it with a toy programming language and a very simplified analysis problem -- just checking if all variables are initalized. While the idea is interesting and might be developped into a tool in the future, the toy task presented in this paper is too simple to warrant an ICLR submission. Just detecting whether a variable is initialized in a string is a toy algorihtmic task, similar to the ones solved in a number of paper in recent years by models such as the Neural Turing Machine, Stack RNNs, Neural GPU, or Differentiable Neural Computer. All these architectures perform almost perfectly on a number of algorithmic tasks, so it is highly probable that they would also solve this one. Unluckily, the authors only compare to much more basic models, such as HMMs. Since the code for many of the above-mentioned models is available online, a paper without these baselines is not ready for ICLR. Moreover, there is a risk that existing models already solve this problem very well, making the contribution unclear.
sampled: The submission presents a modest technique for improving variational autoencoder quality, based on additional ELBO optimization after initialization from q network predictions. It also proposes Jacobian vectors for interpreting variational autoencoders, which is an interesting direction. The Jacobian-based embedding idea is appealing, since Jacobians seem to extend the notion of embeddings from linear models to deep latent Gaussian models. The paper would be stronger with a more direct comparison between Jacobian vectors and prior context-specific embedding methods, including Neelakantan et al, Efficient non-parametric estimation of multiple embeddings per word in vector space, Chen et al, and A Unified Model for Word Sense Representation and Disambiguation. As presented, the experiments do not convince me that Jacobian representations offer a clear advantage in context sensitivity over earlier work on such embeddings. The additional ELBO optimization is also interesting, but it remains underdeveloped in the current version. In particular, the paper does not clarify the compute and accuracy tradeoff between increasing q network complexity and applying extra ELBO optimization steps after the q network prediction.

original: I read the paper in some depth and the idea has some potential, however, the main claim is not substantiated well. sampled: Dynamic Partition Models studies distributed representations through binary encoding, with the goal of producing compact, interpretable representations by explaining data points via partitions of variables into expert supports. original: The paper proposes a convergence analysis of some two-layer NNs with ReLUs. It is not the first such analysis, but maybe it is novel on the assumptions used in the analysis, and the focus on ReLU nonlinearity that is pretty popular in practice. The paper is quite hard to read, with many English mistakes and typos. Nevertheless, the analysis seems to be generally correct. Overall, the paper looks like a correct analysis work, but its form is really suboptimal in terms of writing/presentation, and the novelty and relevance of the results are not always very clear, unfortunately. The main results and intuition should be more clearly presented, and details could be moved to appendices for example - that could only help to improve the visibility and impact of these interesting results.
sampled: PixelVAE is an important and interesting submission that combines a hierarchical VAE with PixelCNNs for natural image distribution modeling. The PixelCNN–VAE combination is valuable, but the novelty should be stated carefully, since the PixelCNN paper had already suggested combining PixelCNN with a VAE. The discussion of hierarchical VAE latents is interesting, particularly the association of high-, mid-, and low-level variation with different latent stages. However, this analysis is not especially surprising, and task-based evidence that PixelCNN improves VAE latent representations would better support the claims about what the latent variables encode. The main weakness is clarity of presentation, especially in the model architecture. original: This paper presents a few interesting ideas, namely the idea of keeping around a set of "danger states" and treating these states with some special consideration in reply to make sure that their impact is not neglected after collecting a lot of additional data. However, there are two main problems: 1) the actual implementation here seems fairly ad-hoc, and it's not at all clear to me that this particular algorithm (building a classifier with equal numbers of good and danger states, and then injecting an additional reward into the Q-learning task based upon this classifier), is the right way to go about this. The presentation is also difficult to follow, and the final results imply aren't that compelling (though this is improving after the revisions, but still has a way to go. Pros: + Interesting idea of keeping around danger states and injecting them into training Cons: - Algorithm doesn't seem that well motivated - Presentation is a bit unclear, takes until page 6 to actually present the basic approach.
sampled: Emergent Predication Structure in Vector Representations of Neural Readers pursues a worthwhile goal by examining recent reading comprehension work through the lens of logical or predication structure. I appreciate the effort to organize models such as Attentive Reader, Stanford Reader, Attention-Sum Reader, Gated-Attention Reader, and Attention-over-Attention Reader into the categories of “aggregation readers” and “explicit reference models.” The paper is generally well written, and section 3 is particularly helpful: the discussion of predication makes the framing clearer and more useful than a broad appeal to logical structure. The shift in terminology from logical structure to predication is appropriate, and the authors’ clarification is detailed and useful. That said, I still have some uncertainty about the paper’s contribution, since the current analysis does not fully show what the predication perspective adds beyond a descriptive organization of neural readers. The abstract’s reference to the Who-did-What dataset is relevant to the paper’s objective, but I remain unsure whether this dataset is well suited to that objective, especially in light of prior concerns about the CNN/DailyMail dataset associated with Chen et al. at ACL’16.

original: This is a strong submission regarding one of the most important and recently introduced methods in neural networks - generative adversarial networks. The authors analyze theoretically the convergence of GANs and discuss the stability of GANs. Both are very important. To the best of my knowledge, this is one of the first theoretical papers about GANs and the paper, contrary to most of the submissions in the field, actually provides deep theoretical insight into this architecture.
